speechtext:
Just by way of introduction I may say that the international convention for the protection of industrial property, which was signed on behalf of Canada at The Hague on November 6, 1925, by a representative of the Canadian government of that day, was ratified by the governor in council by order in council P.C. 648, which was passed on April 19,1928. So far as Canada is concerned the convention came into force on May 1, 1925.
The original Trade Mark and Design Act of Canada was enacted by the parliament of this countiy in 1869, the second year after confederation, and it has remained upon our statute books since that time without material changes. By the British North America Act, 1S67, Canada is authorized to legislate for the regulation of trade and commerce, and under section 132 of that act Canada -can legislate also to give effect to treaties made with the British Empire, to which Canada is a party. Article 10b is of this convention to which Canada gave adherence provides that the contracting parties are bound to ensure the persons entitled- to the benefits of the union effective -protection against unfair competition:
Every act of competition contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters constitutes an act of unfair competition.
Industrial Property

The following acts among others shall be prohibited:
1.	All manner of acts, of such a nature as to create confusion by any means whatsoever with the goods of a competitor;
2.	False allegations, in the course of trade, of such a nature as to discredit the goods of a competitor.
That is a general provision. The convention then provides certain obligations on the part of Canada with regard to respecting the trademarks of foreign countries which are in use in this country, and there is a reciprocal obligation on the part of some twenty nations to respect Canadian trademarks and Canadian tradenames.
This bill, after the second reading, was referred to a special committee of the house. I was selected by the committee to act as its chairman, and the committee had many sittings. It received and heard reports from various parts of Canada, on the measure, which really deals with trademarks and tradenames, and is a remodelling of the Trademark and Design Act of Canada.
I am very grateful for the cooperation of the various members of that committee who gave very serious consideration to the matter, and finally unanimously reported this bill in the form in which it now appears. There are, I find, one or two slight corrections to be made in the printing, but the bill as it stands is the unanimous product of the committee. After representations were heard, and after a full discussion, a number of amendments to the original bill were adopted. I therefore ask the cooperation of this committee in the consideration of this bill, which is the best that we can produce under the circumstances. It does provide one very essential thing-protection of trademarks in this country. Where duplicate trademarks have been in vogue in times past, entitled to equal rights, we have left the courts to decide such matters; but after this bill becomes law, trademarks which are registered in this country shall apply to all Canada and shall apply to Canadian products abroad.
During the consideration of this measure we received representations, very favourable indeed, from those who were dealing in Canadian products in foreign markets, highly appreciating the fact that we were proposing a measure which, so far as we were able to do so without making the legislation retroactive, would in future provide that the trademark on any Canadian goods sold in a foreign market would represent the goods which it purports to represent, so that those in this

country who produce goods of a high standard and quality will have the benefit in the foreign market of the reputation which their goods have really earned.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 22 inclusive agreed to.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 61, to amend the Companies Act.
He said: This amendment to section 85 of the Companies Act is intended to remove confusion which has prevailed since the passing of an amendment to section 63 of the Bankruptcy Act, which is chapter 11 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. The Bankruptcy Act provided that assignments of book debts should be void unless they are registered locally under provincial legislation in any province where legislation had been passed requiring such assignments to be registered locally. Since that date, every province which has a bills of sales act has amended its legislation so as to provide for the registration locally of those assignments of book debts. The banks and all other Canadian companies have complied with those provincial laws.
Recently the question was raised under section 85 of the Companies Act, which provides under section 85 (1) (c) for registration with the Department of the Secretary of State of a floating charge on the undertaking or property of the company, whether the registration of such floating charge did not include the registration of assignments of book debts, and since then some doubt has prevailed about the matter. Canadian companies which have been making such assignments believed they were fulfilling the letter of the law when they complied with the provincial statute. It has seemed to me unnecessary to provide that there should be sent to Ottawa and registered with the Secretary of State assignments of book debts which have already been registered in local registers throughout the length and breadth of the land. To do this involves greater expense, creates confusion and serves no good purpose. Therefore I have introduced this amending bill to provide, in effect, that this subsection of the Companies Act shall not apply to a floating charge created by a company, after the date hereinbefore in this subsection mentioned, on its accounts receivable or any of them.
The purpose of the bill is to avoid all confusion and to provide that the course which has been followed now for a term of years throughout Canada, namely, the registration at the local registry office, shall be effective, without duplicate original assignments having to be filed at the office of the Secretary of States.

I do not
know whether the matter comes under this act or some other provision, but is it not possible for the federal government to exercise some control with respect to financing, issuing of stock, over companies that secure dominion charters? speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the sale, not the issue.

The difficulty that the provincial authorities experience is that they cannot interfere with stock sold under a dominion charter, and there does not seem to be any supervision; these stocks can be increased and sold apparently without let or hindrance, whereas if a company has a provincial charter, there are restrictions upon its activities in this respect. I do not for a moment mean to charge companies with doing this deliberately, but their stock gets into the hands of brokers who seem to be able, when there is a dominion charter, to carry on this practice without hindrance.

It is not control over the issue of a charter which the hon. gentleman deems desirable; it is control over the sale of stock by companies after they have been incorporated. I differ somewhat from the suggestion of the hon. gentleman because I think we keep a closer supervision over the issue of dominion charters than most of the provinces do over the issue of local charters. Time and time again, when we refuse to issue a charter with certain provisions which we deem objectionable, the applicants apparently find no difficulty in securing from provincial governments charters containing the very clauses which we consider objectionable.
Will my hon. friend specify a case?

Take the consolidation in connection with the company to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) called attention the other day: they obtained a provincial charter which contained all the objectionable provisions to which the hon. gentleman referred. But in order to meet the situation, either last session or the session before, the Minister of Justice, who I notice is not in his seat, introduced an amendment to the criminal code which his department deemed sufficient to enable the
[Mr Cahan.J
attorney general in any province to take proceedings against those who indulged in those objectionable proceedings with respect to sales of which the hon. gentleman complains. This parliament amended the criminal code by introducing a new provision, and it was pointed out at that time to the respective provincial governments that, if they deemed this new provision of the criminal code inadequate, the Department of Justice was prepared to consider further amendments which would enable the attorneys general to prosecute offenders in connection with the sale of stocks of companies incorporated under dominion statutes. I have one remedy in mind, and although it may be a purely personal opinion, I have urged it continuously for the last twenty years: I think it is entirely objectionable that under our constitution the conduct and direction of prosecutions for offences under dominion statutes should be taken out of the hands of the attorney general of Canada, who is deeply interested in the maintenance of federal law, and in every case vested in the departments of the attorneys general of the provinces. I think sooner or later the time must come when by some amendment to the constitution, or by some other arrangement, provision may be made that the duty and responsibility for the enforcement of federal laws will rest upon the Attorney General of Canada, who is also Minister of Justice. Until such time I do not believe the condition in this respect will be satisfactory.
Does the minister include the enforcement of the criminal law?

There is a wide division of opinion in that connection. The fact is, however, that attorneys general in the provinces do enforce the criminal law, and I think generally speaking they enforce it very well indeed. I have in mind, however, the passing of special enactments by this parliament involving penalties. It is very seldom-at least this has been my experience-that attorneys general in the provinces can be induced to undertake the enforcement of these specific federal statutes. I believe this is a matter well worthy of consideration.

I am discussing the point
only to obtain the benefit of the minister's experience. I am under the impression, however, that the federal government does appoint attorneys to prosecute under special acts passed by this parliament. Let us consider, for instance, the revenue acts, those measures concerning illicit stills. We know the federal government looks after such prosecutions. I

Companies Act
am under the further impression that certain offences against statutes concerning the Department of Agriculture are enforced by direct prosecution on the federal government.

Has my hon. friend ever
represented the federal government in any such prosecution?

No; I have been so long in parliament, compared with the time I have been at the bar, that I have not had occasion to appear in such prosecutions. I do know, however, that the federal authorities prosecute in matters concerning illicit stills, and the smuggling of cigarettes. I believe, also that the Dominion government prosecutes in connection with a bill which was amended in this house last year and which had to do with the quantity of fats to be found in milk. I am quite certain there are many such matters concerning which the attorney general of Canada appoints special prosecutors. I should like to ask the minister this question:	Where
would he make the distinction?

I was not attempting to
draw a close distinction, but I am of the opinion and my experience has taught me that the enforcement of federal statutes through attorneys or counsel appointed by the federal government is a matter not of right but of complacent acquiescence on the part of the attorneys general of the provinces or their representatives. I have never acted for the Dominion government in any case, but I have endeavoured by laying informations to enforce the criminal law for private parties. In every case, however-and I am speaking of my experience in the city of Montreal-the direction of such prosecutions was really taken out of my hands. The provincial appointee representing the attorney general of the province, would sit alongside me in the courtroom, and say, "I am authorized by the attorney general of the province to represent him in this prosecution. I should be very happy to have your assistance, and to cooperate with you most cordially." He would always add, however, "The responsibility is mine, and in the final result I must exercise my discretion."

I should like to remind
the minister that for many years the matter of the enforcement of federal laws has been under discussion. I can remember when this parliament passed legislation which had no effect whatever because it was not enforced by the provinces. I can remember when the observance of the Sabbath day was under discussion, and that in that connection there
was a wide difference of opinion between people in the province of Ontario and those in the province of Quebec. After the bill had passed in this house an amendment was added to it in the Senate, to the effect that the enforcement of the act would be left to the attorneys general of the provinces. There is no doubt that some dominion legislation comes more or less within the rights of the provinces, and that the enforcement of federal statutes must be left to the attorneys general of the provinces.

Mr. Chairman, while I am interested in this particular phase of the discussion, I must say that I have not received the information I wanted. In the provinces under what is known as the blue-sky law a company has to go to a board, and has to secure from it consent to issue stock. We will consider, for example, a company which has the right to issue stock to the value of a million dollars, and which has issued stock to the .value of only half a million dollars. To all intents and purposes the smaller sum is all the capital required for that particular business. Suddenly, however, they decide to issue the balance of the stock, and have to appear before the board and give reasons for their action. The board takes upon itself the responsibility of saying whether or not the company is entitled to issue additional stock for the purposes of its business. Not only that, but if a new company takes a charter and asks for a licence to do business in the province, it also must appear before the board and obtain a licence to issue stock up to a certain point or a certain given amount which it may require. I am not complaining about the precaution taken by dominion authorities in connection with issuing stock to the extent of $2,000,000 when only $1,000,000 is required. But I do think there is something further required, because it is evident that in two cases with which we are all familiar, an implement company and a packing company, the stock issued was altogether, beyond the capital requirements and as a result those two companies find themselves in serious difficulties to-day. I do not suppose anybody is to blame. The companies simply took advantage of their charters, but the unsuspecting public who bought stock are undoubtedly going to suffer. I must confess I could not persuade my colleagues that we needed something of this kind, but I have been asking for some supervision by the federal authorities to prevent the issue of stock beyond the actual requirements of the
Companies Act

business. It may be said that that is undue interference by government, but if we are to do business under private auspices I know of no other way of checking this practice.
You would provide a federal board?

I would provide a federal board from which every company with a federal charter should secure a licence to issue stock. Prosecutions are necessary undoubtedly, but I do want to see some control over the issue of stock by companies doing business under federal charters.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is now some twenty odd years since I first discussed this matter in this house. I had a very strong opinion with respect to the matter then, I have a very strong opinion now. But if the hon. gentleman's ideas are given effect to, it involves the creation of a board, or court, or commission, or tribunal, which shall have power to pass upon the necessity for each capital issue and upon the character of each capital structure. Against that was urged at the time by friends with whom I discussed the matter this objection, and it is a fairly sound one, that by setting up such a tribunal with the powers indicated, the granting authority to a company to issue stock or to create forms of securities as part of its capital structure would imply that we had given such company a certificate, which involves us in guaranteeing indirectly that it was a sound enterprise in which to invest. I will illustrate that point in this way. A little less than a year ago I made certain observations with respect to a company, and certain people said at once that the government had guaranteed that the shareholders in that company would be protected far beyond what they themselves had stipulated for; in other words it was going to make them better off than they made themselves, because we said we would protect them to the extent we endeavoured to do. That illustrates the soundness of the contention namely, that there is always danger if you set up any federal or provincial tribunal, and it authorizes a given step to be taken, that it thereby implies that that step is a sound one and that the securities issued are worthy of being purchased. We have to go further than that; it is not far enough-yet, it is too far.
Is that not already done in the case of insurance companies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No. Insurance companies are incorporated, as the hon. gentleman knows, under a standard act, which pro-

vides that under certain circumstances they will be authorized to do business. Banks are another illustration. That is, if a certain amount of capital is forthcoming they shall be qualified to transact business. This is an entirely different matter from that to which the hon. gentleman is now referring.
Are we not trying to do this very thing through the utilities commissions of the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am going to mention that. In several provinces this method is being tried, and yet the greatest evils I know of in connection with the sale of shares, in one of the provinces at least, has come under these very circumstances, because the mere granting of authority to sell shares is not the cause of the trouble. It goes deeper than that. The representations made to secure the sale 'of the shares is what becomes of vital importance, and the circumstances under which the capital structure of the company is created.
I am going to endeavour for a few minutes, if it is not too tedious to the committee, to deal with the matter, both from the standpoint of the provinces and the dominion. Each province under a decision of the privy council has power to create a company that may carry on business not only within the province incorporating it, but beyond the province; but each province can restrain and control the sale of shares only within its own boundaries. It therefore follows that a company created in Alberta, and authorized by the utilities board to sell its shares at a given price, may go into the neighbouring province of, we will say, Saskatchewan, and the utilities board having a different view of the situation, or having the same view, the shares are sold there. You thus have sales in Saskatchewan, in Manitoba, in Alberta, in British Columbia, and in every part of Canada, it having been held by the privy council that a company might exercise all the powers practically that could be exercised by an individual, if each province passed a statute that had the effect of enabling the company created in one province to do business in another. I am not going into the technicalities of the law.
There is another illustration. The province of Prince Edward Island a few months ago passed a companies act which was intended to secure to the province additional revenue from companies. The province is said to be the Delaware of Canada. Delaware, as is known, is a very small state of the American union, and its company laws are so liberal that you will find thousands of companies

Companies Act
incorporated there doing business in New York. Not only are the company laws of the state of Delaware very liberal, but the authorities make no close inquiries with regard to the relation between capital issue and capital requirements. That situation prevails in Canada: the companies act passed by the legislature of Prince Edward Island is a very liberal one, and hon. gentlemen may recall that it is much more liberal than the company legislation of some of the other provinces. Then you have the other provinces each with its own provisions with respect to companies; in some they are incorporated by letters patent, in some by memorandum and articles of association, and in some by a combination of both methods.
Then you come to Canada. When I first began the practice of my profession we incorporated companies under letters patent under the Great Seal. Then there came an amendment to the law, and we have it now that the incorporation is issued by the Secretary of State under the seal of his department. We added to our companies act certain provisions of the English act which related to the memorandum and articles of association. It will be recalled that Mr. Asquith set up a commission to study the w'hole question of company law. The late Sir Frank Cust, who was regarded as the leading company solicitor in the kingdom, gave to this matter a tremendous amount of time and energy. The result was that they drafted as good a companies act as it was possible to secure. We copied part of that into our Companies Act. I think one remedy we might avail ourselves of that we have not thus far is with respect to provisions regarding the amount of capital that shall be paid up before a company begins to carry on business. As it stands now, what is done is done perfunctorilj'. The result is that the authority to carry on business is really no protection at all from the federal standpoint. With respect to the provinces, as I have said, the usual provision is that a company may carry on business when ten per cent of its stock is subscribed for and paid up; some merely require that it shall be subscribed. So you have capital structures created that vary from time to time in ways that I will not trespass upon the time of the committee to discuss.
The two cases to which the hon. gentleman has just referred are cases of reorganization. Shortly put, the methods of reorganizing companies are these: First, the assets of the company are valued, and very often the appraisal shows their value to be far in excess of the capital stock outstanding. In the second case, auditors report upon the average earnings
of the corporation over a period of years. For the sake of argument let us say they averaged 12 per cent. Then it might be an appropriate thing to recapitalize the reorganized company on a basis of twice the former capital, because with its former earnings the company would be able to pay interest at 6 per cent upon twice the amount of capital stock formerly outstanding.
Without any real necessity for new capital.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am coming to that. The third point usually considered is the method by which the property is mortgaged to the hilt by a bond issue involving a minimum interest charge since bonds secured by mortgage constitute money loaned to the corporation, not money contributed as a partr ner but money loaned, which establishes the relationship of debtor and creditor. This is loaned at a low rate of interest, for the sake of argument we will say 5 per cent. Then the balance that remains enables a larger issue of common or some other form of stock to be made, and as the hon. gentleman just observed, as a result you have a very large issue of shares. When you have added to that the no par value provision, which I think has worked very badly in this country, if I might venture a criticism, and which is my personal opinion, has been injurious to the whole financial structure of the country, then you have the situation about which complaints have been made.
The question is how we are to remedy the difficulty. In the province of Alberta they passed a law which enabled them to charge with fraud those who made issues of capital stock, let us say, very much in excess of what was reasonably required. One case went to the privy council. It was felt on the one hand that this legislation constituted an interference with dominion powers, because the provincial officers could enter and search the premises and books and institute proceedings of a character peculiarly criminal. Nevertheless, the privy council sustained the action taken by the provincial authorities in that regard. That does not get us any further, however; that only enables the province to-shall I say-successfully raid the books of enterprises that have been promoted with an undue regard for the promoters and a disregard for the rights of the shareholders. That is not any good to the minister.
The other point of the hon. gentleman is that to institute proceedings does not get money back to the shareholders; they have lost their money. In my own view I differ from my hon. friend the Secretary of State. My
Companies Act

opinion is that the point urged so strongly in this house by the late W. F. Maclean is sound, namely that there should be soime machinery by which the federal government can maintain prosecutions for violations of federal statutes. As it stands now, none but a provincial governmental authority may prefer an indictment, which is made either in the name of the attorney general or the crown prosecutor, as the case may be. If he sees fit, for reasons good and sufficient to him, to file a nolle prosequi it follows that the case is not proceeded with. That question became acute in this house in the days of Sir John Thompson, when the prosecution of Connolly and McGreevy was under consideration. It will be recalled that the Dominion government employed very eminent counsel for the purpose of maintaining that prosecution, but the indictment had to be framed and the charge drawn and submitted to the grand jury in the province of Ontario through provincial governmental institutions and by the officials of the attorney general's department.
It will be recalled that in the United States they have federal officials and a federal marshal, the marshal of the United States. They have a federal court and also what amount to federal prosecuting attorneys, who carry on prosecutions for breaches of federal laws. That is a provision which the framers of our confederation avoided for two reasons. In the United States they have forty-eight different kinds of criminal law, and the difficulty of having each state make its own criminal law, in connection with extradition and other similar matters, made it highly essential in the judgment of the framers of our constitution that we should have a universal criminal law, as we have. The second reason was that the administration of justice was felt to be a local matter which local authorities were better able to maintain and carry on than would be the federal authority. So at the moment in this country we have a universal criminal code applicable to every province, but its administration is in the hands of the officials of nine different provinces.
Under those circumstances it is my personal view that we should have a combination of the systems prevailing in the United States and in Great Britain. In Great Britain the department of public prosecutions is undoubtedly the finest organization in the world for the administration of criminal law. Every junior official of the treasury, who is a barrister, who is appointed to a position in that department is a man of promise who, without taking silk, may look forward to being promoted to the bench. Two of the 
greatest of English criminal judges to-day, one the senior member of the bench and the other a more recent appointment, were public prosecutors who gained a very great distinction by reason of the prosecutions they carried on. If any of the members of this house have read the book by the late Sir Harry Poland, who was the oldest practicing member of the bar, they will recall his description of a public prosecutor. The public prosecutor decides whether a case shall be proceeded with, and no political considerations govern. The selection of the local prosecutor rests with him, and he is in control of the whole machinery. The law is put in motion and the matter is carried through to the end by the intervention of the public prosecutor. Sometimes I think that in connection with controverted elections, for example, the only way to get rid of many difficulties is to have an independent tribunal which will have no interest in sawed-off election petitions; this might get over the difficulties which have been experienced. If we had a public prosecutor charged with responsibility for the administration of justice as far as federal statutes are concerned, we might get over some of the difficulties I now see. I observe that my mind has not been working along the same line as that of the Secretary of State. As I have observed the difficulties in connection with the administration of justice with respect to federal statutes, and then realized that the entire power with respect to the administration of justice and the setting in motion of the machinery for public prosecutions rests with provincial officers, at times I have concluded that the method suggested is the one by which the matter can be best dealt with.
On the question of the capital structures of companies, to get back to what the hon. gentleman has been discussing, prosecutions do not serve the purpose he has in mind. I can recall that when I was much younger than I am now I thought the difficulty could be overcome by the setting up of a federal tribunal that might exercise powers similar to those which have been given the Board of Railway Commissioners. I thought possibly it might be a branch of one of our federal commissions. But a country must not be overcommissioned, and already there are some signs indicating that people think we have as many commissions now as are necessary, if not too many. It might be an adjunct of the tariff board, for instance, in the mind of my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) and some of the other hon. gentlemen who think as he does, but the difficulties in the way of setting up a tribunal that gives its imprimatur, its approval and its authority for a certain

Companies Act
course of action to be taken, are not to be overlooked. I am sure, from what the hon. gentleman has observed in connection with other matters, that he will agree that this is an argument not to be lightly set aside. I am satisfied that we must devise some method by which to prevent the reorganization of enterprises as it has been going on in this country. About that I have not the slightest doubt in the world-not any. I am sorry to say-I think it was done inadvertently-that in 1930 we put a direct premium upon doing it. There were, I think, only two members in the house who observed it, and I know the government did not think it meant what it did; but it did permit the reorganization of every business enterprise in this country, if they wanted to do it. That was the effect of that statute.
What was that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The provisions of the statute that permitted the absorption of profits in reserve by reorganization of the capital structure. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will recall what took place. That brought about a tremendous amount of reorganization. The result was that where a company had a capital of 10,000 shares and reserves that would enable it to recapitalize and reorganize, and to issue
15,000	shares, it was done. And the results sometimes were very injurious to the whole situation.
I can only say this to my hon. friend. The life of a government is very uncertain. This is one of the matters to which, however, I have given as much thought as I could in the time I have had at my disposal during the last few months. I think something must be done in the way of federal legislation to prevent just the difficulty to which he alludes. The effect is this-and it does not require any argument, for every hon. member to follow it: A successful company that by reason of great care and thrift has accumulated large reserves, proceeds to capitalize them, with the result that the public, who might hope to get a cheaper product by reason of the company having no greater demands upon it for fixed charges, suddenly finds itself confronted with trebled, quadrupled, or sometimes-I do not know of the apt word to describe it-twenty times its former capital, and the necessity becomes apparent to everyone of providing earnings to take care of a dividend upon its shares perhaps twenty times as large as previously prevailed. This is what the hon. gentleman is aiming at, and whether it can be done without a conference with the provinces I am free to say I have grave doubts. My own conviction, if it is worth anything to the hon. gentleman, is this. If we ever get back to normal conditions, there are two things that are essential for the maintenance of our commercial life, and one is that so far as possible there should be uniformity with respect to the incorporation of companies as between the dominion and the provinces. When I say uniformity, I mean that a company denied incorporation on application to the Secretary of State's office here, should not go to some other office in a province and obtain all the powers and more, as is frequently the case, that were sought for in the federal department.

It has been done in every
case in which I have refused it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To my knowledge, it is
done frequently. Secondly, and this is the more important, the reorganization of companies must be controlled where the public are as vitally interested as they are here. Where enterprises with small capital have been able to make great progress, they must be prevented from issuing enormous waterlogged securities upon which the public pay enhanced prices for the purpose of enabling them to retain those securities so that they shall be quotable or saleable in the markets of the world.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Macleod says "hear, hear." Well, it is easy to say "hear, hear," but much more difficult to say "there, there," when you try to do it; it is a matter of first rate difficulty. When I say that the question of watered stock is one that has engaged the attention of every legislature in the world since 1862 or thereabouts, when we first had our Companies Act,-and companies are merely partnerships with limited liability that create, by reason of the statute, an entity called a corporation rather than a partnership-one realizes how essential it is that some steps should be taken. It is all very simple to sit down and suggest that something be done, but it is very difficult to begin to take action, having regard to the fact that we have a federal constitution, under which the provinces enjoy certain powers and the dominion others. However, I should like the hon. gentleman to know that I am not only in sympathy with what he says but that I believe it must be done. I believe we must discover, by conferences between the provinces and the dominion, some means by which that action shall be taken; and if we get back to normal times during the period I am pri-
Companies Act

vileged to direct the government of the country, I propose that a conference between the provinces and the dominion shall discuss the question to see whether we cannot arrive at some conclusions that will prevent a repetition of the enormous injury that has been done the country as a whole, and the great losses that have been sustained by individual investors by reason of the circumstances to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

Does not the Prime
Minister consider it possible to take steps to prevent the watering of stock in companies that have federal incorporation, even if the federal jurisdiction does not extend to companies incorporated in the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Secretary of State
has alluded to the difficulty. The moment we undertake to impose such restrictions they at once say, "We will not incorporate with you at all but will go to the provinces," as in fact they do. That has been the difficulty to which the Secretary of State has directed attention. He says it is universal; when he refuses them, not being satisfied with the capital structure, or being of the opinion that they do not comply with the provisions of the law, they go to the province. Half a dozen sections in the Companies Act would remedy the difficulty. But that means that no companies would be incorporated here; and in support of that, you have the Secretary of State saying that in every case where he has refused them they have gone to a province and obtained a charter. That has been the real difficulty.

The Prime Minister will remember that after the board was appointed in Alberta the effect was in the opposite direction; they could not get charters there and if they did not they came to the dominion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Exactly.

This is what I was complaining about to the former Minister of Justice during the past eight or nine years. I have only one difference of opinion with the Prime Minister, and it is this. This, of course, is a legal matter and I confess that I have not a legal mind; but if the federal authorities can control banks, insurance companies and large corporations of that character because it is in the public interest-perhaps control is not the proper word, but exercise some medium of control-then it does seem to me that the government would not be assuming any serious responsibility by setting up such a board as is suggested. This, after

all, would obviate criticism of the government in the event of some company, which had a certificate from the board, going wrong. With respect to most of the public business that is done in the country by companies, by whatever means they are set up, the government of Canada and the provincial governments must assume some control or we shall drift into another state of affairs which in my opinion will not prove a huge success, namely, the nationalization of all our public business; because I confess I am not yet convinced that we have arrived at the stage where that would be a desirable thing to have happen. I am convinced that we have arrived at the stage where governments must set up some authority which will prevent the manipulation which now goes on by private individuals and corporations. Legal gentlemen will know the difficulties to be overcome but I contend that if we are to prevent complete nationalization, and I wonder sometimes if it would not be successful, it is necessary that we have some power to deal with the evils which have crept in, particularly during the past few years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Section 91 of the British North America Act, dealing with the powers of parliament, in part reads as follows:
-it is hereby declared that (nothwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,-
15.	Banking, incorporation of hanks, and the issue of paper money.
16.	Savings banks.
17.	Weights and Measures.
18.	Bills of exchange and promissory notes.
19.	Interest.
20.	Legal tender.
21.	Bankruptcy and insolvency.
In connection with banks and other corporations, to which the hon. gentleman has referred, this parliament has exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the matter as well as with other matters affecting savings banks, bills of exchange, interest and legal tender. The courts have held that inasmuch as insurance companies may have provincial incorporation as well as federal there is no exclusive jurisdiction resting either with parliament, on the one hand, or the legislatures on the other. If we had exclusive jurisdiction with l'espect to all corporations, as we have with respect to banks, then there would be no difficulty. It has been held that insurance companies-one of the matters referred to by the hon. gentleman-do not require licences from this dominion to enable them to transact business in a province, and that their incor-

Companies Act
poration or licensing by one province will permit them, under proper conditions, to do business in other provinces. This illustrates the difficulties with which we have to deal due to the joint control of the dominion and the provinces. These difficulties have caused all our trouble up to the present moment although there is a way out which I have not ventured to express because it would not be the expression of a mature opinion on my part. I do believe that we can meet this difficulty and I promise hon. gentlemen that if it is not met it will not be because of any desire not to do so.

In reply to the criticism
offered by hon. gentlemen-

It is not.
criticism, it is information we are after.

I do not intend to cast any reflection upon my predecessors when I say that the administration of the Companies Act since August, 1930, compares favourably with its administration at any other time since the act was placed upon the statute books. It has been honestly and efficiently administered and-1 am prepared to refute any adverse criticism thereon. I do not think hon. gentlemen have realized the many ramifications of this subject. I, as Secretary of State, may refuse to grant a charter to-day; within forty-eight hours, an application may be made to London and a charter granted within sixty-four hours. Under the comity which exists between us and Great Britain, the company granted such a charter could carry on business in this country. I have seen that done time and time again when there were restrictions under our act to which the applicants did not wish to submit.
Would a company incorporated in London have all the powers and authority granted to one incorporated by the federal government?

There are extraordinary
powers granted under the English companies act which are not granted under our act.

My hon.
friend did not get the point of my question. Would a company organized and granted a charter in London under the English law have the same right to do business, in the province of Alberta for example, as a company organized and granted a charter iby the dominion?

Quite so. It simply makes formal registration and then proceeds to do business. Under the English companies act a
man may be incorporated to do in the name of a company almost everything that can be done by an individual. There would also be the greatest difficulty under the comity which exists between us and the United States. We could hardly declare that an American company could not come in here and do business unless its capital issues were subject to revision here. These companies come in by the hundreds and thousands and do business throughout Canada. They do not take out provincial or federal charters, they are incorporated in Delaware, New Jersey, New York or some other state and -they come into Canada and carry on their corporate activities without regard to the restrictions imposed upon Canadians by our Companies Act. There is a wide range to be investigated in undertaking remedial legislation.
I do not think the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) understood what I said about the administration of justice in the provinces, because I think my ideas are somewhat in accord with his. If there is any constitutional method whereby the agents or officers of this government can be authorized to enforce federal laws against over-capitalization and the breach of federal legislation in regard to companies and the government will authorize me to take action at the expense of the government, I shall see that such action is taken. The matter is rendered far more difficult by -the constitutional issue discussed by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power).

I recognize the difficulties with regard1 to jurisdiction but may I remind the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that when it was proposed that we should have bank inspection it was argued that that would be dangerous 'because the dominion might possibly 'be forced to accept certain responsibilities which it would not want to accept. There was an instance in which there was absolutely no doubt that the dominion had exclusive jurisdiction.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES

speechtext:
Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for an extension of time from 31st August, 1932, to the 31st August, 1934, for the construction or completion
C.N.R.-Branch Lines

of certain branch lines of railway of the Canadian National Railway Company, authorized by chapters 19, 20, 21, 25, 28, 29. 30, 32, 33, 34, 35 and 36 of the statutes of 1929.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Manion thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 70, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for an extension of the time for the construction or completion of certain lines of railway.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second times and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.
On section 1-Extension of time for construction.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: What is the number of this bill?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I am afraid the bill has not yet been given a number, 'because, with the consent of the house, we are making more rapid progress than is usual. The bill is merely for an extension of time for the building of various branch lines, twelve in number, that have not yet been completed. The bill introduced in 1929 permitted an extension for three years to August 31, 1932. As that time will run out on August 31 of this year, this is merely giving the railway a further extension of two years for the construction of these lines, without in any way saying that it will necessarily be two years before they are constructed. That is the whole purport of the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I realize that is the purport of the bill and I am not sure whether the authority is absolutely necessary; possibly it is. I have, however, before me a protest from at least one part of our western community against this further extension in completing some of the work that has already been undertaken. Some of these branch lines have been carried almost to completion. The one about which the protest to which I refer has been made has had the grade constructed.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: Which one is it?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
The Hemaruka-
Scapa line in Alberta. The grade is constructed, the ties and steel laid, the crossings put in, the telegraph poles erected and the wire strung, but the line is left unballasted, and because of that there has been no movement of freight of any kind from the Drum-

heller coal fields or from Calgary distributing points to the residents living along that line. That road serves a large part of my constituency and the people there find it necessary to bring their coal and other freight eastward on the Goose Lake line to Saskatoon and then back by Biggar and Loverna, a distance of some 320 miles further, just because this line has not been ballasted; at least that is the excuse offered by western district superintendents. Last year I had the privilege of corresponding with the district superintendent of Saskatoon and again with the divisional superintendent at Winnipeg, and in each case the statement was made that the line was not ballasted and they could not carry our coal.
I have no great objection to this extension of two years, but if it is just a matter of stalling off the work for two years, I do not know whether it is worth our while putting this bill through the house. When so much money has been expended as has been the case in this particular instance, the matter of ballasting the line to carry our coal and other freight to needy settlers should be undertaken and completed. The total mileage of this line from Hemaruka to Scapa is some forty-one miles. The residents of Loverna district point out to me their whole difficulty would be solved if the line were ballasted at present from Hemaruka to the Youngstown-Coro-nation line. Then by coming north and crossing this line at a point about six miles west of Hemaruka they claim, if this were ballasted, their coal and other freight coming from Drumheller east could switch north from Youngstown to Hemaruka and move eastward to Loverna and surrounding districts. What I wish to emphasize in connection with this particular line is that the ballasting of the whole road should be gone on with if at all possible. I know the minister can use the argument that funds are not available. That may be true, but I would remind him that just the other night he had some estimates put through for improvements for the Trent and other canals that are not nearly so important, and in each of the several cases there was a considerable increase of expenditure over that of the previous year. Therefore the argument that funds are not available is not going to be very weighty in this case when one considers that ballasting a matter of six miles of line will provide for the residents of some hundred or more miles of territory a much cheaper commodity. I am informed by the residents of that district that their coal costs them an average of $1.60 a ton more if they have it brought in by Saskatoon, and as a result many of them go north on the

Canadian Pacific and get their coal at $1.60 a ton cheaper. May I suggest to the hon. member that a refusal to pass this bill would not necessarily hurry, in fact it would delay, the completion of the line. I have not any quarrel with the hon. gentleman in regard to the completion of this line, but in this bill there are twelve lines which it is claimed are in exactly the same position. The balance involved in these undertakings amounts to $13,000,000, which under 'present conditions is quite a sum. As regards the line to which my hon. friend refers, the figures that I have show that the total expenditure plus 15 per cent, which is the leeway allowed, was to be $1,650,000. The amount spent is given to me as $806,000, which is just a little less than half of the total amount. I mention that merely in passing. Perhaps it may help the committee to understand the whole situation if I say what I have said many times before in regard to various branch lines which have been brought to the attention of the government and the railway, that the railway management at this time take the attitude that because of the very serious financial situation and the continually decreasing earnings, they do not believe any amount should be spent on most of these lines, that is the twelve different ones affected. If conditions improve I am sure the government would be quite pleased; certainly they would have no objection to helping the railways to make the extensions required. At the present time, however, there is the feeling that the Hemaruka-Scapa line is on all fours with other branch lines, some twelve in number, and involving an expenditure of abolit $13,000,000.

I appeal to the minister

The gradients run from -8 to over per cent, and the alignment is unequalled in any similar length of road anywhere in the country. By continuing the railway from Guysborough around to Mulgrave you will be able to do away with the operation of that most expensive section, on which a large amount of rolling stock has been destroyed; and only about 25 per cent of a normal load can be carried over it. I think the minister's department should consider this practical suggestion. What I am anxious about at the moment is to get some understanding from him that he will complete the section of the road, 72 per cent of the construction of which has already been done.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I have very much pleasure in supporting the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley). every sympathy for both him and my hon. friend from Pictou. They have both placed the matter before me a number of times. subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I expect you to promise me a little more than you did the other day.

speechtext: If this bill goes through will these lines be finished within the next twelve or fifteen months?

speechtext: Is it not a question whether the railways are not losing more money by not putting down the rails than will be saved by this policy?

speechtext: Then I suppose it would be useless for me to press further for the Mafeking cut-off?

speechtext: I am afraid so.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: I am quite sincere in that statement. The hon. member for Pictou mentioned the value, in the matter of the relief of unemployment, of the Sunnybrae-Guysborough line, and I am equally sincere with regard to the Mafeking cut-off. I do not think my hon. friend from Pictou is a very good salesman. He is trying to sell the idea of completing this branch line of his by knocking the construction of another line. I do not think there are many successful salesmen who try to sell their goods by knocking other lines. I may tell my hon. friend that his prophecy with regard to the Hudson Bay railway will not be fulfilled if the government give the line sympathetic consideration and if proper insurance rates are obtained.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: We are giving it sympathetic consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
One thing at a time is a very good rule. During the fall of 1931 it was my good fortune to visit the port of Churchill, where I had the privilege of a conversation with the commanders of the boats, the Farnworth and the Warkworth, which carried the two shiploads of wheat from Churchill to the old country. They told me that on their voyage into the bay they experienced no difficulty whatever; in other words it was a very humdrum sort of trip. They simply sailed through the straits into the bay and loaded their ships in the harbour, and I have never heard that they experienced any difficulty on the return journey. The fact that they did not do so is shown by their safe arrival in the old country. I could give more of their conversation, but to do so would be to make an invidious comparison with another port of Canada, and in that I do not propose to follow my hon. friend from Pictou, who has endeavoured to fulfil his desires by belittling another route. Ships have been going into and coming out of Hudson bay for two hundred years or more, and there have been very few failures. It is true that the season is short; it may not be .as safe as some other routes, but I would point out to the committee that until the last few years there were no aids to navigation along that route. Now that condition has been rectified, and if one is to believe the two commanders who brought their ships to that port, there is absolutely no difficulty whatever in making that a very navigable route in certain seasons of the year.
May I say here that we Canadians are usually prone to talk about our immeasurable resources and how we may expand this country. Why any one part of Canada should feel that the opening of another port is going to be to the disadvantage of the country rather than to its advantage passes my comprehension. If Canada is the country we think it is, then the development of the port of Churchill will work to the benefit of the whole country. If we are going to adopt in Canada a narrow, provincial attitude and contend that the country can prosper only by the development of one portion or the other, then I am afraid all our prophecies in regard to this country have been made on a wrong basis.
With regard to this government giving sympathetic consideration to the Hudson Bay railway and the port of Churchill, with the Minister of Railways I feel quite safe in saying that this government has not only given sympathetic consideration but has carried to
completion the railway and the port, and today this route is ready for business. All that is needed is for the shippers to send their goods to Churchill, and they will get to the old country.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: The last sentence of the minister's remarks contains the whole picture; all that is required is for the people to send their grain through Churchill, and why the deuce don't they? Last year the minister had to go over the country with a fine tooth comb looking for cargoes; the minister did everything and implored everybody to send some grain over that route. Those are the facts, and they can be verified by Hansard of last year. My objection is that the minister proposes to find $2,000,000 this year for Hudson bay but be cannot find a dollar to complete a short section of an eastern route. With regard to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, who has just spoken, if he will read up the history-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: Ancient history.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: -of Hudson bay and its navigation, he will find that in one year out of three the Hudson's Bay Company either did not get their yearly ship into the bay or, if they did get it in they did not get it out. That is a matter of histopf. The difficulty has not been the lack of aids to navigation; it has been that the port has been icebound, and it will be icebound again. Through the grace of God, or the weather condition last year a condition prevailed that has not prevailed for fifty years, but you cannot count on that every year.	[DOT]

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES

I think the grace of God is fairly well exhausted as far as helping out the Hudson Bay railway is concerned. About all the dividend we get from that road is the enjoyment we derive in discussing it in this house. Certainly I would not belittle any legitimate enterprise in this country. The east contributed as much as any other section of the country to the development of western Canada, and all I am asking to-day is that a reasonable amount should be spent to complete a road which is now seventyrtwo per cent completed. The amount for which I am asking is small in comparison with what is being spent to-day on the port of Churchill. That is all I have to say about that. If anyone else wishes to make further remarks as to the navigability of Hudson bay, or to say anything about that part of the country

as a summer resort, I shall be glad to hear him and give the matter respectful consideration. For my part, however, I have made up my mind fairly well, from history I have read as to conditions governing both Hudson bay and James bay, that there will not be very much grain or any other commodities moved out of the port, however much you may spend on it.

speechtext: Are the connecting links from Elk Point with the Saskatchewan line along the Saskatchewan river in the same category as the other lines? Mr.*MANION: Yes; that is all that it is proposed to spend at the present time.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext:
I was interested in the remarks of some hon. members in regard to the Hudson Bay railway. This is not a party question. Both parties are tied up to it and we have spent $50,000,000 of the people's money. I submit that it is our duty to put our best foot forward to see if we cannot make practical use of the railway, instead of condemning it after spending this money on it. It is, I re-

peat, the duty of every member of this house to do everything possible to make that railway a success. I am not condemning it nor saying that it will not be a real shipping route, but after we have spent $50,000,000 on it we should try to make it a success.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR CONSTRUCTION OR COMPLETION OF BRANCH LINES
speechtext: I do not intend to enter into any argument about the Hudson Bay railway. Some years ago we exhausted our oratory on the question and finally both parties were convinced that it should be undertaken. What I wish to direct attention to is the fact that at least two-thirds of the money involved in that project was raised by a tax on western land. I call it a tax advisedly, because homestead land was sold to the extent of $37,000000 to contribute to a fund used for the building of the Hudson Bay railway. So that it is not all money taken out of the public treasury in the ordinary way.
