maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know I am not, but I
wanted His Honour to say so to prevent my being cut off later on.
The matter which I intend to discuss is in connection with the Department of Fisheries, which has decided to inaugurate in British Columbia a system of inspection of canned salmon. British Columbia is the only province affected by this matter. The salmon canning industry as a whole is in accord with the idea of having canned salmon inspected. This industry is a very important one, last year's catch being valued at close to $17,000,000. There are directly employed in this industry some 12,000 people, and probably as many more are indirectly employed. When dependents are considered, it will be found that something like fifty or sixty thousand people are vitally interested in this industry, and this is my excuse for bringing up the matter.
I believe the idea of inspection is to help the sale of canned salmon in foreign countries, and also particularly in Great Britain. We hope to be able to say to Great Britain: If you will give us a preference we will guarantee you a first class article and demonstrate it by government inspection. With this principle I heartily agree, but I submit that the method proposed to be adopted is a poor one and calculated to frustrate the very object for which it is designed. In this connection two orders in council have been passed, one providing for the inspection and the other constituting a board of inspection. These are numbered P.C. 723 and 724, and these orders in council cause me to consider for a moment the difference between passing legislation and orders in council. I do not think the provisions which appear in these orders in council would have passed the house or the fisheries committee had they been brought down in the form of legislation. I desire to comment on one or two details in the orders in council, and then I shall proceed to discuss my main objection thereto.
Subsection (c) of section 26 of P.C. 723 is comprised of one sentence of 235 words, and consequently it is extremely involved. Among other things it states that certain provisions shall apply only when the salmon is shipped
from a cannery or private warehouse connected with a railway, whereas these provisions should apply to all shipments. Another provision of this subsection is that each day's pack shall be identified by code markings. That is a necessary provision, but it should apply to all salmon to be inspected and not only to salmon shipped out of a private warehouse. Another provision is that railway cars loaded at such canneries and private warehouses shall be sealed before they are despatched. Who would ship a carload of salmon valued at from three to eight thousand dollars without having it sealed? It is not necessary to pass an order in council to provide for that, the common sense of the railways and the cannery officials will see that such a car is sealed before it starts on its journey. The provision should be that the car shall be sealed by the inspector, otherwise it is of no use.
I am unable to find any provision to guarantee that the cases inspected are actually shipped. I may be visited by an inspector; he comes into my warehouse and I point out a thousand cases of salmon; he inspects those cases but puts no mark or stamp upon them. He tests a certain number of cans and then tells me I can ship them; he goes away without seeing them shipped and if I desire I can ship five hundred cases of that lot and five hundred cases of a lot not inspected. All that is required is that the cars shall be sealed, and that would be done by the railway officials in any case. Subsection (d) of the same section reads:
Application for inspection of any parcel or parcels of canned salmon shall be made in writing to the chief supervisor of fisheries for the province. Inspection shall be made as promptly as possible, but the Department of Fisheries shall not be responsible for any delays.
That is entirely too vague; the shipper should have some protection that his goods will be inspected within a reasonable time. A delay beyond a reasonable period might half ruin him. As is known, many of the canneries are much indebted to the banks and they have to finance on a very close margin; yet a man's inspection may be held up perhaps for a week, without any obligation on the part of the government except that they will do it when they feel like it. Of course the provision is "as promptly as possible". I submit that should be within four days.
In the same section is laid down the method of getting the inspection started. The man has to apply in writing to the chief supervisor. Then the chief supervisor, when he feels like doing so, reports to the board of inspection.
Canned Salmon Inspection

The board, when they have spare time from their other duties, because they have other business to look after as they still carry on their own affairs, get busy. After they have made their inspection, they report back to the chief supervisor and the latter reports to the owner. This is a great deal of unnecessary red tape when prompt inspection is necessary. We are trying to accelerate business, not to hold it back.
Then we come to section 29 (d), which deals with the way in which the salmon is to be inspected. There is a different procedure in regard to 100 cases from that in regard to 10,000 cases. The question of cost is not involved, because the cost is so much a case; it makes no difference as to cost per case whether 100 or 10,000 are inspected at one time. This provides that if you take out 100 cases at a time and have them inspected, twelve cases, or 12 per cent, are withdrawn. But if you have 10,000 cases, only ninety-six cases, which is a good deal less than one per cent, are taken out. Then one tin out of each such case is opened. The result is this: if you have 100 cases of salmon tested and inspected at the one time, one tin out of 400 tins will be opened and tested. But if you have 10,000 cases tested, only one tin out of 5,000 tins will be inspected. Why the difference? The quality is not likely to be any poorer if you take 100 cases than if you take 10,000, but in one instance the proportion is one out of 400 and in the other one out of 5,000. I do not think our British friends will consider adequate an inspection based on one out of 5,000 tins. Under the act dealing with canned fruits and vegetables, the inspection is three per cent. Of course I would not for a moment suggest that that proportion should be taken for salmon, because the cost would be prohibitive, but there is a tremendous difference between that and taking one tin out of 5,000.
Section 30 provides the way in which the inspection is to be paid for. It is to be paid for by a fee at the rate of one cent per case, this to be charged by the board of inspection and collected from the owner of the fish. Also in certain cases expenses of travelling and living are charged. I shall deal with that later on, but before I proceed I want to emphasize the point that it is a most unusual and phenomenal procedure that the canner is to pay for the inspection of his products. I question whether under the act there is any authority for this. I think it is section 4 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act which provides that the governor in council may make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions

of the act. That is the usual clause. Under that they have taken power to impose a very heavy charge upon the owners of these fish. I question very much and I submit to the minister and the ministry whether that is legal under the Meat and Canned Foods Act, because it is well understood that regulations must be consistent with the act and they cannot make any large and violent departure from its provisions.
As regards section 24, I shall not take time to go into it. It is only a matter of bad drafting, but as it reads at present it does not make sense. I shall say just this, and it will be on record: The words "except as herein otherwise provided" should be struck out at the beginning and inserted after the words "provided that" in the third last line. That deals with all the minor matters, what I would call the technical points in the regulations.
I shall turn now to the requirements of the inspection. We find the first one in regulation 27(a):
Canned salmon that are found by the board of inspection to be fresh, firm, well packed and in good merchantable condition shall be approved and a certificate in the form attached marked "A," shall be issued therefor.
What do we mean by the word "fresh"? What would the ordinary man on the street mean by the word "fresh" applied to fish? Would it not mean fish that had been anything but canned? I do not quibble about dictionary meanings, because you get various definitions, but the dictionary term is "not preserved by salting or by pickling, canning, etc." How can fish that has been in a can for three months be described as fresh? The language used in the Meat and Canned Foods Act, the original act, is "sound, wholesome and fit for human food," which I think is a better definition. According to the regulation, however, if the board of inspection finds the fish is "fresh, firm and well packed," the canner is given a certificate, the only one granted. No other grade or quality gets a certificate. To that form of certificate, there is a serious objection which I shall deal with later on.
What happens if the fish is not up to the first grade on which a certificate is granted? Section 27 (b) provides that if it is not up to that, but if it is "sound, wholesome and fit for human food," then it can be sold but it is not entitled to a certificate. What is the difference between "fresh, firm and well packed," and "sound, wholesome and fit for human food"? I cannot see much. If, however, the fish comes under the second category, that is "sound, wholesome and fit for human

Canned Salmon Inspection
food," it does not get a certificate but if stamped "second quality" on each tin, it may be sold. It may also be "reconditioned" for re-examination. What does the word "recondition" suggest to our minds in connection with fish in a can? My mind goes back to Upton Sinclair's novel, The Jungle, in which were described conditions, now long past, it is to be hoped, in the packing houses in Chicago. When they came upon a mass or a boiling of meat that was so bad it actually stank, and would not pass muster in any case, they reconditioned it by doping it with benzoic acid or salt petre or some other strong preservative so that it was practically embalmed. An embalmed corpse does not smell and they then sold it as canned beef. Is that what the word means in this case? The word "recondition" is used, and I do not know any other meaning for it. IIuw can we change something that is "sound, wholesome and fit for human food" into "fresh, firm and well packed"? I do not know how you can make canned salmon firm that is not already firm; I do not know how you can change it into being well packed unless you empty the fish out of the can and repack it, which course would be absurd on account of the cost. There is an important point I want to note here: there is in this order in council no provision for condemning rotten fish, let us say, on the first inspection. Only if it has been reconditioned and re-examiDed and is then found unfit for human food, can it be condemned. Mark you, it is based on that. The man whose fish will not pass first quality is privileged to recondition ic. If he brings it up again, and it is then found to be rotten it can at that time be condemned- but only then. That in my view is a foolish regulation.
Section 27 (d) reads as follows:
Canned salmon that are found after reconditioning and reexamination not to be up to "second quality" shall be confiscated

An so on. In my opinion it ought to read:
Canned salmon that are found not to be up to "second quality" shall be confiscated.
It should not matter when the defective condition is found. I notice further that if the fish is condemned the owner cannot sell it for fox meat. On the other hand, however, the government could have it for its own use, or sell it for the use of animals. If it is condemned and put into such condition that it cannot be sold for human food, I think the owner should be in a position to get what he can for it as fox meat.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the order in
council No. 723, of which I was speaking this afternoon really provides for only two grades of canned salmon. The first grade is not called No. 1 grade, it is not called first quality. I presume it would be called certificated, because it is entitled to a certificate which declares it has been inspected, and is "fresh, firm and well packed." The second quality is anything under that, which is found to be "sound, wholesome and fit for human food." It does not get a certificate, and it must have the words "second quality" stamped on each tin. The question also arises as to stuff unfit for human food, but I think the department will see the point I made this afternoon and will provide for its being condemned whenever it is seen, whether on the first or second inspection. At present the question only arises if it comes up for re-examination.
We will assume that inspected salmon will fall naturally into those two grades. I will put the two together to make the comparison easier. One is "fresh, firm and well packed"; the second is "sound, wholesome and fit for human food." Now, one of two things is going to happen. These distinctions are so fine that it is almost impossible to distinguish between them. What member of this house who is not familiar with the subject will say which of these two definitions he would prefer as characterizing the best grade: "sound wholesome and fit for human food;" or "fresh, firm and well packed"? If sound, wholesome and fit for human food, it must also be fresh, firm and well packed; and I suppose, inversely, if it is fresh, firm and well packed, it also will be, or should be, sound, wholesome and fit for human food. But I think what he would prefer would be a distinction more explanatory and more likely to come home to the housewife as indicating the better quality of the two grades. But the order in council reads otherwise. The chances are that the two definitions will get so merged in the mind of the inspector, that anything that is sound, wholesome and fit for human food will also pass as No. 1 and get the certificate; in which case you have a very expensive system of inspection which will only be a farce. "What's the use? It is all going to be classified as No. 1." On the other hand, we will suppose the inspector being a very experienced man, with these two definitions-to our minds so little removed from each other-can see a distinction between them; and we will suppose he certifies 20 per cent as being under No. 1, but
Canned Salmon Inspection

nevertheless sound, wholesome and fit for human food. Then this 20 per cent will only be permitted to be sold if it has embossed on each tin in letters of a given size the words "second quality." You will find this in paragraph 27, subsection (c).
I protest against that policy. It will involve a heavy and a very unjustifiable loss upon an industry that is having great trouble at the present time to keep its head above water. Why? Because the wrong word is used. When you use the words "second quality" you simply damn the sale of everything so marked. There is nothing about which the human mind is so sensitive in connection with food as any suggestion that there is anything wrong with it, as fish, especially with respect to tins of canned fish; that it is something a little less than superior, a little less than first quality. You only have to put that idea into the mind of the housewife or purchaser-and you certainly do instil that idea when you mark on the tin that the contents are of second quality-and she says "no." In her mind or that of her husband the suggestion arises of ptomaine poisoning, and everything that that stands for, and they say, "No, even if it is going to cost a little more, we will pay the extra to get the genuine government guaranteed quality." Even the poorest of our people in institutions would object to that "second quality" fish, and if some got the tummy-ache they would blame it on the second quality fish, and you would have a scandal.
This suggestion of second quality appears so much more forcibly in the case of tinned fish than anything else. I think in Great Britain butchers are compelled to indicate that their mutton is frozen New Zealand mutton as distinguished from the home product. The housewife sees the mutton so marked, and she can gauge whether it is of a quality that satisfies her, and very often the only difference is that of price. But in that case she sees it; her eye is her informant, so to speak. Take second grade potatoes. The purchaser looks at the potatoes, it is only a question of cutting off the diseased pieces, no one will be poisoned, it is only a question in the housewife's mind if it pays to buy second quality potatoes. As I say, we use the wrong words when we prescribe this marking of "second quality." Let us take cheese and butter. While they do use figures, 1, 2 and 3. they do not apply the word "quality"; these articles are simply graded 1 and 2 and 3. But there again the purchaser has at least an opportunity of seeing, and sampling what she is buying. But take eggs; you cannot

sample them. There are three grades before you come to No. 2-specials, extras and firsts, and then the fourth grade is seconds. There are three grades to sell the better class quality before you come to the second. Then take a another comparison that is most applicable to canned fish, that is canned fruit and vegetables. Regulation No. 15-it is taken out of the same act, Canned Meat and Foods Act- prescribes that there shall be four grades of canned fruits-fancy, choice, standard and second. There again, sir, we have three descriptions not calculated to offend the eye or mind of the purchaser before coming down to the second grade.
It would be all right if we marked this fish "Canada choice" and "Canada standard" the same as fruit is marked. That would give the cannery man a chance to sell a considerable portion of his pack which might ibe assigned to second quality grade, but the consumer would be absolutely protected because it is not permitted to stamp the container "second quality" unless the fish is found to be "sound, wholesome and fit for human food." What more do they want? Why condemn this commodity with the suggestion that it is second quality, and therefore inferior quality, when "choice" or "standard" would do equally well? It would not penalize the cannery man, and -the consumer, as I say, would be absolutely protected.
There is another aspect of considerable danger, not from the point of view of health, but from the success of the inspection system -which is what we are trying to get at, or else there is no use doing it at all. The government certificate says: The contents of this tin have been examined, and they are fresh, firm and well packed. It says nothing about variety at all. There is as much difference between varieties of salmon as there is between hon. gentlemen who sit on the right and the left of you, Mr. Speaker; as much difference as there is between lamb and goat meat. In fact there is more difference than that, and perhaps I might give an illustration to bring it home more clearly. I will not talk about prices to-day, because the price of salmon today is just what you can get for it, and that is very little indeed. In the days when salmon was selling on a fair market basis the comparison would be like this: The best brand of salmon, sockeye, would be selling at $19 a case, while the lowest grade, the name of which I will not mention, would be selling for $5 a case or something like that. That gives an illustration of what the market considers to be the difference between certain varieties, -both first class in their different

Canned Salmon Inspection
ways. I have authority for that in section 24 of the Meat and Canned Foods Act, which
says:
For the purposes of this act the varieties of British Columbia salmon shall be designated, and, if the need for such is established to the satisfaction of the governor in council, graded as provided in the regulations.
The act says they shall be designated. Is that designation to be put on the chicken house or in the family bible? Do you not think the place clearly indicated is on the can itself? It should be designated as being what it really is, and the authority is contained in the act itself. It is true that the government certificate only says the contents are fresh, firm and well packed. The government say they will not go beyond that and will not be bound by anything more, but you must understand the argument that will be advanced by the wholesaler, trying to push his goods on to the retailer, and by the retailer trying to sell them to the housewife. She will be told that the government of Canada is behind that product. This is the argument that will be used: "You cannot go wrong in buying this, because posted here on the shelf is a government certificate which says this is the best you can buy." That is what it will be interpreted to mean, because the housewife will not walk over to the shelf and read it in order to find that it only says the salmon is firm, fresh and well packed. She will take the word of the retailer for it; she will think it is the best salmon because the retailer says so. Then when she gets it home and opens is and finds it to be a lower grade, though still fresh, firm and well packed, what will she think? It will not be what she thought she was buying; it will be the So stuff instead of the $19 stuff, and that will lessen sales instead of increasing them. She will say, "This government inspection thing is all a joke; this is not the kind of salmon we have been getting at all." It will be a detriment instead of an advantage.
I might give a true incident out of my own experience, which occurred after I was married and came out from the old country. I suppose we possessed the ordinary intelligence of people of the old country, accustomed to bright red salmon and knowing nothing of the food values of the lower grades. We bought a tin or two of salmon and found the contents, instead of being red, to be a dirty white colour tinged with pink at the edges. I do not mean that it was unclean or that its food values were not comparatively high, but it was a dirty looking product. It looked unpalatable, and we jumped to the conclusion
that it was off quality. We were suspicious and very afraid, so we thought we would try it on the cat, that if it did not kill the cat it would be all right for us. It did not seem to hurt the cat at all, but then we remembered that a cat is supposed to have nine lives, and we thought perhaps we had not exhausted them all. If we fed the cat enough salmon to. demonstrate on all the nine lives we would have no salmon left; and if the cat then died we would be out both the cat and the salmon, so we threw away the salmon. I have no doubt that being a Canadian cat, and possessed of more sense or at least more knowledge than we had, it went around the corner, dug up the salmon and had a fine time eating it.
That illustrates how a person who knows nothing of the substantial food values contained in these lower grades may be led away.
I find on page 36 of a market report issued by the department some months ago the following words:
.Retailers express the opinion that the grade and quality of canned salmon should be clearly marked on all labels. It was even suggested *that labels should distinguish between early and late pack.
There is some little advantage in the one as against the other.
What is the remedy? It is very simple one. We already have the word "Canada" on the tin, and I would suggest that we put the word "choice" and then the name of the variety. Then we would have on the tin "Canada choice soekeye" or "Canada standard sockeye," whatever the grade might be. There is further authority for that in section 15 of the fish regulations, which provides:
British Columbia salmon when packed in cans shall be designated as follows:
I will not take time to read the five designations which are mentioned one by one. The name of each is given, together with the kind of salmon that may be included under that grade. It is provided elsewhere in the act that British Columbia salmon shall be designated; here is a designation ready to hand, and we only have to use that designation and put one of those five names on the tin, coupled with the word "choice" or the word "standard" as the case may be. Then the housewife will know she is getting what she pays for; she will know she is getting a grade of salmon certified by the government, and she will get the grade that suits her purse and her inclination. If she buys sock-eye she will know she is getting the best salmon she can buy, and if she buys one of the lower grades, which some people think
Canned Salmon Inspection

was packed into the car and the door shut and sealed-we did not need an order in council to do it-rushing to get the railwayman to sign the bill of lading, and then speeding up to the bank with the bill of lading, to make good a draft that had already been obtained. It is absolutely necessary that there be a sufficient number of men to do this quickly. The government should pay and control the inspectors as it does in other industries. The department was created two or three years ago to foster the fishing industry; it certainly was not created to hurt it. The sales tax has been increased, a duty has been put on tin which has hurt the industry without benefiting the tin man because his factory is in the middle of Canada, so why burden the industry with another $22,000? No other industry has to bear a burden of this kind. In addition to all this, the industry undergoes heavy taxation in other ways, such as licence fees, case taxes, and so on.
I shall deal with the arguments which no doubt will be raised against my contention. It will be argued that the cannery men are agreeable to these regulations, that they were consulted and were unanimous. If a meeting is held of 500 people and they are asked if they are in favour of good government, everyone would say yes, but if you ask them what they consider to be good government, there will be 499 different methods given for achieving that end. That is the situation which exists in this case. There were 60 canneries in operation last year, and I should like to know how many were represented at the meeting. I should like to know if they were really unanimous, because I have certain knowledge that some were not present. They agreed to the general principle, but who would not? There is no doubt it is a highly desirable thing, but there are differences of opinion as to the methods of carrying it out. I could quote the, opinions of a couple of cannery men, but I shall not take the time. I have in my hand a copy of the draft proposal made some months ago by the canneries, also a copy of what was proposed and submitted to them and copies of the orders in council which were passed. The three documents do not agree; there is a difference of opinion on substantial points. What is it about which the cannery men are said to be unanimous? Was it their own views, as expressed in their memorial; was it those submitted to them, and which have since been changed, or was it the provisions of the orders in council? The cannery men may not as yet have seen these orders in council, or if they have, it is only just recently.
[Mr. Neill.3
Even supposing the cannery men were unanimous, which they were not, what about it? Two or three years ago this house, the pension officials and the pension commission were all agreed that we had the very last word in pension legislation. We acclaimed the fact that we had at least settled a difficult problem, but what happened? In less than ten months it was found that this was not the last word in legislation, that it did not work out as all of us hoped it would. It is possible to be unanimous about what you do not thoroughly understand, and the cannery men should be given an opportunity to consider this matter. They may be unanimously in favour of inspection, but have they been advised by their lawyers and managers as to the effect of these regulations?
Another argument which will no doubt be used is that even though this may not be exactly right, it should be tried out for a year. This is a new departure, something which we do not make very often, and it should be started right. It will be a lot easier to start right than to retrace our steps later on.
Let me summarize in a few sentences the points to which I wish to call attention.
In the first place, there are too few inspectors to do justice to the cannery men who must have prompt inspection. There are too few inspectors to obviate the suggestion of favouritism. If an inspector condemns a large portion of a man's pack he should have the right of appeal to a board consisting of more than three men. Secondly, the only provision for the condemning of fish is in connection with reconditioned fish which is then seen to be unfit for human food. Thirdly, the words "second quality" should not be permitted to appear on the can, as it would kill the sale of a perfectly good article of food. If this item is insisted on, it will put a heavy handicap upon the cannery men. Fourth, as the government certificate will be taken to mean that the article is of the very best, there may be a misapprehension on the part of the customer. The salmon should be rated as being " standard " or " choice " of a particular named variety, of which there are only five. Lastly, the system of having inspectors appointed and paid by the cannery men should be done away with.
It will be said that this is destructive criticism, but I state again that I have nothing but approval for the principle of inspection. However, I want to see it a workable system, and the cannery men do also. I am quite willing that my remarks in connection with these particular orders in council should be considered as destructive criticism. We do

Supply-Indian Affairs
not need an architect in this case, we -need a wrecker. A sound edifice cannot be built on a rotten foundation-let us wreck the rotten foundation and start to build an edifice which will be a benefit to the industry and a credit to the department. The regulations do not go into effect until June 1 and there is time fo-r reconsideration. They should be explained to the cannery men so that their viewpoint -may be obtained, and then an effort made to evolve a workable system. If necessary it could1 be left over -until another ye-ar has passed. There will not be much bad salmon -put up this year because economic conditions will -make such a practice unprofitable. You get such a miserably low, cut-throat price for the very l>est grade that it would never pay -to put up a -bad grade-you would have to give something away with the tin as well. There is not much danger of the fish noit being good quality this year.
I have endeavoured to keep away from any factious or political criticism, I simply want this matter considered. I am glad to see the former minister present in the chamber; he understands the fishing industry, and if he will look into the matter I shall be satisfied with his decision.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Maloney in the chair.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall not take up much of the time of the committee, but I have a little story to tell. The incident to which I shall refer after three centuries of so-called civilization, is almost as cruel and appalling as those which took place during the days of Indian warfare. I do not intend to be hard upon the minister because he was kind enough the other day to give me some information, but it is my intention to try to prevent a bad appointment being made by the Civil Service Commission. I refer to the appointment of an Indian agent at Cacouna. On September 23 of last year the following letter was sent to the department, addressed to the minister:
(Personal.)
My Dear Sir:	,	.
I herewith enclose a sworn declaration signed by Mr. Omer Dube, ex-candidate in the last provincial election, who complains of political
interference on the part of Mr. Jos. Berube, agent for the Indians, at Cacouna, Temiscouata county.	.
Would you please be good enough to authorize an investigation to be held as to this man s conduct during this last election.	..
Mr. Alphonse Garon, advocate of Rimouski, is appointed investigator for this district for these cases.	.
With thanks for your kind attention, l am, Yours respectfully,
Chas. Eug. Dube.
There is no other letter from that gentleman in the returns tabled in the house. The files have been carefully combed and conscientiously weeded, and following the example of one of the most famous naturalists, Cuvier, who with a single tooth of a prehistoric monster reconstituted its skeleton, I shall try to do the same thing with this case. I wonder if the minister will be kind enough to let me see the original of the letter which was signed by the gentleman and which appears on the file. I hope he will have no objection to doing so later on. With that letter is sent this affidavit, which is very curious:
Riviere du Loup,
September 10, 1931. I, the undersigned, Omer Dube, of Cacouna, solemnly declare that on the 9th of August, while I was candidate in the provincial election contest-
Note those words.
-I saw Joseph Berube, Indian agent at Cacouna, indulge in political partisanship, and he has even, to the knowledge of a great number of electors at St. J. B. of Isle Verte, with other persons upset the hustings on which I was, as candidate-
Note those words.
-addressing the crowd which was present, s	(Sgd.) Omer Dube,
Ex-Candidate.
Sworn before me-
And so forth. Note this again, Mr. Chairman: he called himself a genuine Liberal candidate, It was in virtue of an affidavit given by a so-called Liberal candidate and transmitted to the department by a well known Conservative candidate that the investigation was ordered. But the real fact is that this man has never been a candidate, either Conservative or Liberal, because he has never made in any election the deposit required by law. This is the only publication that he issued during the last provincial election. I am sorry I have no English translation, but I shall read it in French and I am sure the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and all those who understand French will have a hearty laugh at it:
To the electors of Temiscouata North. I have the intention to canvass your votes as a
Supply-Indian Affairs

candidate in this county. Last Sunday, at St-Jean-Baptiste de 1'Islc-Vcrte, I was stoned, pelted with stones, so much so that I ascended to Heaven like Elijah in his chariot of fire; until suddenly, I was crowned by the sun's glorious rays, likewise shall I be crowned at sunset on August 24.
I give warning to my opponents that I shall carry on an honest and courteous fight.
Awaiting the evening of August 24.
J. P. 0. Dube,
Straight Liberal Candidate, Cacouna.
The fact is that he was not a candidate at all. The matter was taken very seriously by the department, and the private secretary to the minister wrote to the Deputy Superintendent General on November 20, 1931, that ample time should be given Mr. Dube in order that he might make arrangements for the attendance of witnesses and the holding of the investigation. He said;
I am enclosing the letter addressed to the minister by Mr. Dube, as 'well as an affidavit completed by Mr. Omer Dube. These may be helpful to the commissioner.
A euphemism for "executioner." He went out with a tomahawk and he was on the warpath. Then the deputy minister writes to the minister that time, not ample, should be given to make the investigation. I am very sorry that the minister acted on the letter that was sent to him, because a man who has not made a deposit in an election is not a candidate. The investigation disclosed some very aimusing things. First of all, it was held on December 4, 1931, and a witness said that the agent had discussed politics in favour of the Liberal party with another person in the store. The agent at the same time is a chauffeur. This will explain something that comes immediately after. According to a letter that I received from his attorney at the investigation, what he spoke about when he discussed politics was a conversation about the price of butter during the election of 1930. If he was wrong then, I do not see why the Prime Minister and all his supporters should not foe impeached. If it is a crime to speak of butter, that is perhaps the reason why all the 'Conservative members were silent while the butter provision was placed in the New Zealand treaty the other daj7. Everything has an explanation. Apparently it was a crime for him to say that the price of butter was low, but he was only repeating what the leader of the Conservative party had said on every .platform in this country. He was blamed for something else, for having made a bet on the result of the election. This was in 1926 and the bet was made after the poll was closed so that it could not have influenced any voter. Someone had offered to bet and he made a bet, but the poll

was closed. As I said, the man was a chauffeur and they blamed him for having driven a voter on the polling day to Bic, in Rimouski county. He was asked by the father-in-law of the voter, who was a Conservative, to drive his son-in-law to Bic in another constituency quite far from there in order that he should not be in Cacouna, Temiseouata county, on the polling day. No one could blame him for that. As a chauffeur he was paid for the trip; nevertheless he was accused of political partisanship on that account. He was simply earning money.
Then there is a complaint from the so-called Liberal candidate who was supposed to have gone to heaven. I cannot say, whether, according to the circular I have just read, he was supposed to go to heaven like the prophet Elijah, when they raised the hustings which fell-a very unfortunate incident. In the report of the investigation there was a note that I find in every report of Mr. Caron, the investigator, to the effect that the accused man did not think fit to make himself heard; so he was guilty. That is contrary to all principles of British fair play and justice.
I have something to ask the minister and I am sure he is fair enough to give me a favourable reply. That investigation took place in the month of November, and on January 13, the Deputy Superintendent General of Indian Affairs wrote thus to Mr. Berube:
I beg to advise you that under the authority of an order of His Excellency the Governor General in council of the 8th instant, your services as Indian agent, grade 2, Cacouna agency in the province of Quebec, are dispensed with on account of political partisanship. I wired you to-day to this effect.
Yours very truly,
Duncan C. Scott.
Another letter was sent to him 'bearing the same da-te, January 13, as follows:
Dear Sir:
With further reference to my letter to you of to-day advising you that under the authority of an order of His Excellency the Governor General in council of the 8th instant, your services as Indian agent, grade 2, Cacouna agency, Que., are dispensed with. I have to say that the order in council states that they are dispensed with as from the first day of January, 1932.
It had a retroactive effect; it was like the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act-peace, order and good government. He acted as agent until the first of February, at which time another appointment was made. Very naturally he asked for his salary for the month of January. Then, on February 13 Mr. A. F. MacKenzie, the secretary of the department, wrote as follows:
In reply to your letter of the 6th instant. I beg to refer you to letter of the 13th ultimo,

Supply-Indian Affairs
and to say that as order in council No. 3 of the 8th ultimo states that your services were dispensed with as from January 1, 1932, the department cannot pay you salary for January.
That, of course, was too late for a Christmas gift. What is due, however, should be paid, and I am now asking the minister if he will be kind enough to see to it that the salary for the month of January is paid. At a later time I shall have something further to say.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Superintendent General of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the hon. member has completed his remarks in regard to this matter. In reply to his question concerning the salary, I may say I know of no provision whereby Mr. Berube can be paid a salary for the month of January when the order in council dispensing with his services was passed to take effect December 31, or January 1.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very sorry, but I shall have to continue my remarks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So am I.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, you may as well take it with a smile. Then followed some correspondence between the deputy minister and the Civil Service Commission asking for the advertisement of the agency. Finally, on February 9, posters were sent out, and on the same date the secretary of the Civil Service Commission wrote to the deputy minister as follows:
It will be appreciated if you will have this competition brought to the attention of any temporary employee who may desire to compete.
The answer of the deputy minister on February 10 was as follows:
I beg to advise you that pending a permanent appointment in the position, Indian agent, grade 2, Cacouna, Quebec, as a result of the competition now pending, it has been necessary to employ an agent temporarily as the services of Mr. Berube, were discontinued immediately on receipt of order in council P.C. 3 of the 8th ultimo. We have engaged Mr. Alexis Michaud under the thirty-day clause. His services began on the first instant. I am enclosing his application also requisition, and would ask that you issue a temporary certificate in his favour.
On February 12 the deputy minister again wrote to the Civil Service Commission as follows:
I beg to advise you that we are informed by Mr. Alexis Michaud who is now temporarily employed as Indian agent, Cacouna agency, Quebec, that his is desirous of being a candidate for permanent appointment. As I know that the applications are received by you up to the 22nd instant and it may not be possible for him to fill an application before that date, it is desired that the application forwarded you with my letter of the 10th instant requesting temporary certificate for him, be transferred to the competition.
It does not appear that after that any application was sent by Michaud to the Civil Service Commission. Michaud's first application, including the signature, was in handwriting, and was declared at Cacouna on January 15, 1932, before the mayor of Riviere du Loup. The document may have been declared worthless by the department, because all in the department know that although municipal officials may have jurisdiction to act as justices of the peace, they cannot so act outside of the municipalities in which they are mayors or councillors.
An answer to one of the returns gives the following information:
When competition 21818 was advertised Michaud entered application with the Civil Service Commission.
He made that application on January 15, and on February 9, three weeks later, the position was advertised. The right answer to the return ivould have been:
After the competition was advertised Michaud entered his application.
And not-
When the competition was advertised Michaud entered his application.
That application was received at Ottawa by the Civil Service Commission on February 18, 1932.
The second application, a requisition for temporary employment, was sworn to at Riviere du Loup on January 21, 1932, before the same gentleman who made the recommendation to the department. It was forwarded by the Deputy Minister of Indian Affairs to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission, together with a covering letter dated February 10, 1932, which I have read, and which was received by the Civil Service Commission on February 11, 1932.
*I am sorry the Postmaster General is not in his seat, but I should like to say that an application was made on January 15 and was received in Ottawa only three weeks after, or on February 18. It seems to me that is a long time for a letter to come from Cacouna to Ottawa. It would take no longer for a letter to go to the south pole or to the end3 of the earth. Usually the service of the department of the Postmaster General is much better than that. The other application' took more than a fortnight to reach the Civil Service Commission, namely, from January 21 to February 11. There is something very strange about this affair. The fact is that the temporary certificate for Michaud was sent by the Civil Service Commission on February

Supply-Indian Affairs

20, and had a retroactive effect to February 1. Berube could not be paid, although he was informed only in the middle of January, and had received no notice from the department before the middle of January, that his dismissal had taken effect. Until the end of the month he had to fulfil his duties as Indian agent, no other appointment having been made. The circumstances in the case of Michaud are somewhat different. The certificate was issued on February 29 for the month of February and also for the month of March. It would seem that he was luckier than the other chap.
I asked the following question:
On whose recommendation did the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs temporarily appoint Mr. Alexis Michaud as Indian agent at Cacouna, Quebec?
The answer to that question was:
Mr. Michaud was appointed as temporary Indian agent at Cacouna on instructions of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs.
I was under the impression that he had been recommended by someone who had known of the vacancy before it was advertised. To my great surprise I received a few days ago the following letter from the gentleman who had sworn to Michaud's application. It is as follows:
Vous auriez mieux fait de m'ecrire et je n'aurais eu aueune objection a vous renseigner.
The English would be:
You should have written to me, and I would have had no objection to giving you the information.
This communication was signed by the gentleman who has the patronage for the Tory party in my constituency. When I asked for information the minister hesitated in giving it to me. As a consequence I would have to write to Riviere du Loup, to that gentleman, to get the information my good friend the minister is supposed to supply. I should think, after the letter I sent to the minister, he would have had no objection to making me familiar with the whole case.
I asked for a copy of all the correspondence, telegrams, petitions and applications exchanged between all persons of Temiscouata county on the one hand and the ministers and officials of the federal government on the other since August, 1930, about the position of Indian agent at Cacouna. The return was brought down containing no papers from Temiscouata with the exception of the applications forwarded to the Civil Service Commission. The

report of Mr. MacKenzie, the secretary' of the Department of Indian Affairs, reads as follows:
March 30, 1932.
As requested I visited Riviere du Loup early in March and interviewed four candidates for the position of Indian agent, Cacouna:
John Dunnigan, David Lebel,
Alexis Michaud, Cleophas J. Sirois.
These men all have fair qualifications, are of good standing in the community, and it is really hard to make much distinction.
This is very nice. It sounds like honey, maple syrup and Gobeil's preserves.
The present incumbent, Mr. Michaud, is in my opinion qualified to carry on the rvork; in fact he has done so with reasonable satisfaction since February 1st.
Reasonable satisfaction is something less than ordinary satisfaction, but it has been so drafted probably because he had been appointed agent temporarily.
The Indians, hov'ever, object to his appointment on the ground that he lives about two miles from the village.
The Indians had to wear their moccasins and snowshoes to visit him two miles away; on the other hand, it was quite troublesome for him to go down to the village in his feather headdress, wearing his wampum belt and all the insignia of his great office.
I might also say that his knowledge of English is very limited; the other three candidates are much more competent in that respect. I do not know', however, that this might be considered much of a drawback as the locality is distinctly French-Canadian. Mr. Michaud found it necessary to speak to me through an interpreter, not being sure enough of his English.
He is the only man against whom there are any serious objections, because, as Mr. MacKenzie says, the other men are all "of good standing in the community, and it is really hard to make much distinction." The whole trouble is that the worst man has been appointed temporary agent, and this is what I protest against. I have no interest in the matter, because nearly all four candidates heckled me at my meetings and voted against me. I stand up to-night for the public interest in order that the Indians may be well looked after, and this can only be done by choosing the best man for the position. But may I tell the minister that the appointment will be temporary, because I take this opportunity of advising him and his colleagues also that with respect to all those whom they have dismissed for what in their eyes is the mortal sin of political partisanship I will see to it that in

Supply-Indian Affairs__________
some way or another they are reinstated when my party comes into power again. So the "permanent" employee will be only a temporary employee until after the next election. Mr. MacKenzie continues:
Mr. Sirois would be a very competent man but he runs an hotel during the summer season and there is objection on this score.
The trouble is Mr. MacKenzie says that Mr. Sirois runs an hotel during the summer season, while Mr. Sirois himself says that he ran an hotel in years gone by. He contends there is no objection now because he is no longer in the business. In fact in his statement he says he was glad to employ Indian waiters while he was keeping an hotel. It gave a picturesque touch in the old days when he was doing so well as host. Mr. MacKenzie adds:
He is also away considerably during the rest of the year in his capacity as a commercial traveller. This absence accounts for his not signing his application for the position, it having been prepared in his absence by his wife.
He speaks very good English, and his wife also speaks very good English. She could very well look after the Indians while he is away.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are they Conservatives?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are all good Conservatives, so my choice would be very embarrassing. I am not blaming the minister. I am confident he does not know the qualifications of the man he appointed. He was simply recommended to him without any reason at all. Now, there is another good man:
Mr. David Label would be quite competent and lives near the village. His father was a former Indian agent. He has a good command of English and French and knows the Indians well.
Well, if it was not his father it was his uncle; anyway, it was in the family. If he gets the job the wampum belt will come back again as a family trophy. Here is something in the report that I regret very much. Mr. MacKenzie says:
Mr. Dunnigan did not impress me so favourably. He has had little business experience.
Mr. Dunnigan is a studious gentleman and is familiar with French and English. He writes and speaks both languages well, and in fact he is a perfect bilinguist.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is he a Tory?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, he is a Conservative, and the next time you see him you will like 41761-162J
him. He is a very nice gentleman for whom I have great respect. I like him a little more than my hon. friend from North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) because he is not so noisy; he is a wise and undemonstrative gentleman. Not one of these gentlemen voted for me. Mr. Dunnigan is a good man; Mr. Lebel is a good man; Mr. Sirois is a good man; Mr. Michaud is not a good candidate. Unfortunately the one chosen does not speak English and is also objected to by the Indians, because he lives too far from them.
The last paragraph of Mr. MacKenzie's report is very strange:
My recommendation would be in favour of either Mr. Michaud or Mr. Lebel.
There are three good men and one bad man, and one good man and the bad man are recommended while the other two good men are left aside. I cannot understand that. If Sirois, Lebel or Dunnigan had been recommended, I would not have spoken to-night, but instead of that Michaud was recommended.
Now let us take up the Civil Service Commission. I suppose they have read the file, but they have not seen Mr. Sirois, Mr. Lebel, Mr. Dunnigan or Mr. Michaud. Having seen them, the secretary of the department says that the two best men are Mr. Michaud and Mr. Lebel. This is unfair, and I hope the minister will see to it that either Mr. Sirois, who is very well qualified, or Mr. Lebel, who told a little fib in saying that his father was a former agent, instead of his uncle, or Mr. Dunnigan, of whom it was wrongly said he had little business experience, is chosen, by the commission on the recommendation of the department. May I say here that I regret very much that no representative of the Civil Service Commission examined these men. All they had to go on was the recommendation of the department. Mr. MacKenzie stayed at the Victoria Hotel, near the station in Riviere du Loup, and the candidates had to meet him there. I wonder if there was not a nigger in the Indian woodpile, who then said to Mr. MacKenzie, "Give a chance to Lebel, who is my most intimate friend. The others will not know that I have recommended him, and the minister is very discreet. He does not leave many letters in the files coming from Temis-couata county. I can trust him, and I think I can trust you to give a chance to my good friend Lebel, even if it is at the expense of the others. They will know nothing about it, and the Civil Service Commission will be blamed for making the appointment. I can say to Mr. Dunnigan or Mr. Sirois that I regret very
Supply-Indian Affairs

much that they cannot be appointed, but I can say the Civil Service Commission appointed LebeL" I do not state that to be what happened, but I think that is the presumption.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let me state what I want carried. To sum up, here we have an Indian agency. The former agent was dismissed after an investigation, on the sworn affidavit of a so-called candidate, a gentleman who really has not been a candidate in any election in this country since confederation, and who is much too young to have been a candidate at the time of confederation. In the first place the investigation was not justified, but when it did take place what w'as discovered? It was stated that the former agent had made a bet, after the polls were dosed, which could not have influenced any voter, and as a matter of fact he wras provoked to do so by one of the candidates. Then it was stated that he talked politics, that he said the price of butter was low. Perhaps he said that to a farmer who wanted a higher price for his butter. That was held to be political partisanship. Then it was said he acted as chauffeur and drove a Conservative voter to another constituency. He was paid for his trip, but he was blamed for that. Certainly those were not good reasons for dismissing him. He cannot be reinstated now until after the next general election, but in the meantime I have great sympathy for the poor Indians. They must be looked after by someone who is able to speak both languages, and. the agent must not live too far away, otherwise the Indians will wear out their moccasins and the department will find it very expensive to buy new moccasins and new snowshoes all the time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Carried.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; I have not yet stated my case. The minister is fair minded and I know he has been deceived. If he had known what I have been telling him I am sure Michaud would not have been appointed temporary agent. But I did not want to impose on the minister by recommending anyone, and in any case it is not my duty to do so. What I want to-night is to prevent the minister from making another faux pas. I cannot be more in favour of one of the candidates than another, because according to an official of the department, three are good and Michaud is not so good. To sum up, I wonder if the minister would be kind enough to let me know if the appointments will be
[Mr Pouliot.]
made soon by the Civil Service Commission, and if he would be favourable to either Mr. Sirois, Mr. Dunnigan or Mr. Lebel rather than Mr. Michaud?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked as to the appointment of the agent, but a sentence or two before that he stated that the appointment was made by the Civil Service Commission. He should direct his question to the body who will make the appointment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will send them a copy
of Hansard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to direct the attention of the minister to one or two matters having to do with Indian reservations in the province of New Brunswick. The first case to which I would direct attention is that of Burnt Church, in Northumberland county, where a change was made in December of 1930 in the person furnishing supplies to the Indians. At that time supplies were furnished at a point within a mile or so of the reservation. Now the Indians have to travel twenty-five miles for their supplies, and I wish the minister would look into that matter.
The next complaint that has been sent to me with regard to the Indians has to do with Big Cove, in the county of Kent, where formerly the Indians obtained their supplies within a mile of the reservation. They now have to travel nine miles, and it is a hardship because these Indians have no horses. In some cases they have to hire horses in order to get to the store where the supplies are given out. I have in mind the case of one Indian whom it cost $12 during the winter to get his supplies. The store at Rexton, where the Indians obtain their supplies, will not send in those goods, according to my information, unless they have a large order which will warrant their sending it in by team. This should not continue. These Indians should not have to pay their own money, especially in these hard times, to get supplies to their homes. I know it is not the intention of the department and I wish they would look into the matter. Another point to which I would direct the attention of the minister and ask for some explanation is this. I put a question on the order paper asking what firms had sold supplies to the Department of Indian Affairs for Indian reservations in the province of New Brunswick in 1930-31. The department laid on the table a reply giving names for 1930-31 and I find on page 4 of the return that the name of Howard Brothers Limited appears as having supplied the Indians in 1931.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is the name?

Supply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Howard Brothers of Sussex. A letter from Messrs. Howard Brothers to me states that they gave no supplies in 1931. The last they gave were in August 1930 and they were then notified that they would no longer be required to furnish supplies. They got their cheque for the August supplies in September, but they appear on this 'list as having supplied in 1931. I would ask the minister to look into this matter. Perhaps it is an error in copying, but at any rate they requested me to bring the matter to the attention of the minister and I replied that I would do so when the estimates were under consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This item now before the house provides for expenses in connection with the administration of Indian Affairs, including salaries, supplies, relief, medical attendance, hospitalization, and so forth, and there is a reduction of $S53,600 as compared with last year. I am wondering whether, in making up this estimate, the department is fully alive to the condition of the Indians in a large part of the country. I speak particularly with regard to the Indians on the great lakes between what is recognized as the Ottawa river district and the boundary line of Manitoba. In this regard, I would say that unless some steps are taken and taken at an early date to provide the Indians with some means by which they can earn their own livelihood, then every Indian in that entire district will have to be provided for in food and clothing. Last year I called the attention of the minister and of the department to what I considered to be the necessity for some arrangement being made between the federal department and the provinces by which the right of the Indians to the natural means of earning their living- that is, taking furbearing animals-would be restored to them.
For more than forty years I have watched the development of the Indians throughout that great country and have noticed a gradual rise in their standards of living, up until perhaps eight or ten years ago, since when they have been virtually driven out by a class of white trapper who has no regard for any law that anjr government can place on the statute books with regard to the conservation or the preservation of animal life in this country, until the Indian has been reduced to absolute pauperism. That is particularly true during this period of economic stress, when it is impossible for the Indians to get employment as guide? or in ordinary vocations in the woods or with mining companies or anywhere else. They have been deprived of their own natural means of livelihood and they cannot compete *with the white man in the only available
avenues of ordinary work now open to anyone. Consequently, unless some steps are taken and taken quickly to provide them with some opportunity to make their own living, the department is faced with two things: Either they will have to watch the Indians starving to death or they will have to provide completely for their sustenance and clothing.
It is impossible to describe the desperate condition some of the Indians are in throughout that country. I cannot speak of other parts of Canada except from what I have gathered from persons with whom I am associated in connection with some of the work carried on amongst the Indians. But in all that country designated as northern Ontario and the watershed of Hudson bay, the Indians have now been reduced to such a state that the Department of Indian Affairs must do something for them or they will starve. They are going down and down. The inroads of tuberculosis, to which they are naturally subject, especially in their present undernourished condition, are so great among them that the Indians will disappear; and as I have said on one or two occasions in this house before, if there is any class of people anywhere for whom the Canadian nation is responsible, it is the native races of this country. I therefore urge upon the minister that a vigorous, determined effort be made without further delay to arrive at some arrangement between the federal government and the provinces, by which the Indians will have restored to them the exclusive right of taking fur-bearing animals.
Having given a lot of thought and study to the question, I say that the matter of conservation in relation to the fur-bearing animals and game birds of Canada will be at once provided for if the Indian is left in his inherent right of taking the fur-bearing animals in that country. There will be no such thing as wiping them out, as the white trapper does, going in with dynamite and other instruments which serve to destroy the sources of supply. The Indian will conserve the fur-bearing animals and the game birds and animals of the country if he is allowed exclusive jurisdiction and is given his natural, inherent right in this regard. That is the only thing the Indians have left to them, and surely we can provide that they be given that right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member has
mentioned a very real problem in the administration of Indian Affairs. Prior to the building of the Transcontinental railway the Indians inhabiting the northern parts of Ontario and Quebec subsisted, as their ancestors had
Supply-Indian Affairs

done, on the products of the chase, and after that railway was built the Indians came from the northerly districts down to the railway and overcame, to a certain degree, their fear, shall I say, of the white man and his civilization, and increasingly they have made their homes along that line of railway. In addition to that, the railway provided necessary facilities whereby the white man who was interested in trapping could gain easier access to that country. Latterly the development of airplane transportation has made it that much easier for the white man to enter that district and denude the country of its game, the natural supply of food for the aborigines.
The hon. member has said that we should take steps to see to it that the natural, inherent right of the Indian to pursue game in these areas should be his. But may I point out to the house that that area is under the jurisdiction and control of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and that the dominion government have no jurisdiction over it, through the Indian department, except as regards those areas which have been set aside as reserves for the Indians, on which they may live and carry on their natural vocations. The department is fully alive to the seriousness of this question. Il has not neglected the interests of the Indians, because hospitals have been built at various points along that railway and large sums of money are paid out annually for the maintenance of residential schools for Indian children.
With regard to the preservation or conservation of game, I am happy to be able to tell the committee that during the past winter the province of Quebec passed an order in council which virtually sets aside all that area north of the Transcontinental railway for the exclusive use of the Indians for trapping. At the present time a game commission in Ontario is inquiring into the preservation of game in that province. It may be, and we hope it will be, that that commission's recommendations in connection with the area north of the Transcontinental railway will follow the example set by the government of Quebec. If that is done, no doubt the Indian will be able to take care of himself just as well as did his forebears. The department is faced with difficulties in connection with this part of the country comparable only to the conditions which exist to a lesser degree in the Northwest Territories. I am not prepared to say whether or not the department has been pursuing the right course, but
IMr. Murphy.]
I am prepared to say that it is the policy of the department to endeavour to put the Indian in a position where he can stand upon his own feet and provide himself with the necessities of life.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Has the department made
any progress in getting the British Columbia government to carry out the bargain entered into in connection with Indian reserves? I understand an agreement, called the McKenna agreement, was entered into, either in 1917 or 1919, which settled a long-standing dispute with British Columbia. A new survey was to be made of the reserves; where it was found a reserve was too large for the use of the Indians, a certain portion would be given up, and in other cases where fishing sites and the like were needed, extra reserves were to be provided. When this had been done an agreement was entered into with the province of British Columbia under which that province was to deed in fee simple to the dominion all Indian reserves, suspending what is known as the reversionary rights. It was agreed that after that was done the Dominion government would have the control of these reserves and if it should happen that the Indians did not need them, they could be sold, a reasonable arrangement being arrived at as to the disposition of funds so acquired. The disposition of reserves not required was also agreed to.
Many of these reserves were in out of the way places, making the survey difficult, but I understand, that it has been completed for some years and the Dominions government is having difficulty in getting the provincial government to implement its bargain and deed over these reserves. In some cases the Indians want to sell their lands; in other cases the lands are needed for public purposes but everything is being held up because the provincial government seems to be either unwilling or unable to deed over these reserves. Is there any prospect of bringing this matter to a head?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Some years ago a commission was appointed to inquire into this matter and a report was made whereby certain reserves were contracted in size while others were enlarged. A survey was made following the recommendations of the commission, and that survey is on file. In order to convey undisputed title of these reserves to the Dominion government in trust for the Indians, it is only necessary that an order in council be passed by the British Columbia government.

Supply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't they do it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That question should
properly be addressed to another quarter. For the information of the hon. member I may say that negotiations with British Columbia are now in progress and have been for some time, but up to date they have not been successful.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to a matter in connection with Indians which affects the people of British Columbia, and perhaps affects the people in other provinces. Reference has been made at various times to the fact that the Indians are in a destitute condition, but I intend to refer to the Indian who might be considered as well off. There are some Indians in British Columbia who might even be considered rich and who in many ways have copied the white man, especially in the ownership of motor cars. Many of them have discarded the now ancient pony and have taken to the motor car. Many of these Indians are careless in driving and accidents have occurred where other cars and persons have been damaged. The Indian, being a ward of the government cannot be sued in the courts, and I should like the minister to give some attention to this angle of this question.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is the first occasion upon which this matter has been brought to my attention, and I shall be pleased to give it every consideration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This matter was brought up last year at the farmers' institute, and I was sent a copy of the resolution passed at that meeting and again at the meeting this year. The feeling is that the Indian is allowed to go free while the white man can be sued.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I fancy there is no part of Canada where the Indian is more seriously pressed, particuarly in the winter time, than in Manitoba. In the original treaties made with the federal government, I think at the time of Lord Selkirk, the Indian was given certain reserves in which to hunt. As these reserves were released for settlement purposes, other parcels of land farther back were provided, and at the present time the Indian is located far away from civilization. Unfortunately, the game had been pretty well cleaned out in these districts. Under the original agreement with the government the Indian had the right to hunt at all seasons of the year not only on his own preserve but on all crown lands, but since the natural resources have been returned to the western
provinces and the provincial game laws are extended to crown lands, the Indian is prevented from hunting thereon. There is no doubt that the Indian is faced with many hardships but as the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has said, he would be able to keep himself fairly well if he were permitted to hunt over all crown lands as well as over his own reserves. As the situation is now, the government of Manitoba, and I presume, those of Saskatchewan and Alberta, have game laws which protect these crown lands so that the Indians have not an opportunity to hunt on them. It would be a matter well worthy of consideration for the minister to see if he could not obtain a licence for the Indians to hunt on crown lands, because that would go very far towards relieving their condition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for St. Boniface says that in the original agreement or treaty entered into between the dominion and the Indians they had certain rights to hunt on crown lands as well as on the reserves which had been set apart for their use. But the natural resources agreement which was entered into between the dominion and the three prairie provinces, if I am not mistaken -and I speak subject to correction-contains a clause under which at the present time an Indian ha.s a right not only to hunt on his reserve but also to take game at any season of the year if he requires it for food for himself or his family. The hon. member shakes his head, but I have the natural resources agreement in my room. I am going to ask a messenger to get it, and I shall read the clause.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Only for food.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said for food. Therefore my statement is correct. That is the point I understood the hon. member for St. Boniface was making. Thus the rights which the Indian had at the beginning are now increased because he may take that game whenever he finds it if he or his family require it for food.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I may be in error but
several bands in Manitoba from time to time have appealed to me; I have had occasion to take the matter up with the provincial government following the transfer of the natural resources and if I am not mistaken, Hon. Donald McKenzie, Minister of Mines and Natural Resources of that province, gave me to understand that the provincial game laws would apply and the Indians would not be permitted to hunt.
Supply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would be
permitted to hunt for food.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am afraid some of those Indians unfortunately are not aware of that fact. I know they have been stopped by the game wardens when they were hunting for food on crown lands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Recently in the Calgary
police court an Indian was proceeded against under the provincial game act for killing game. Judgment was rendered against him, and I believe an appeal has been entered. So that in one instance at least judgment has been given against an Indian for shooting game on crown lands.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know several instances
in Manitoba where Indians have been put in gaol.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So far as
