hunting by Indians is concerned, I presume hon. members are speaking of exclusive right, because my experience in Alberta is that they hunt over any land they feel inclined to hunt over, until they are put off.
I should like to ask the minister why he has so completely and radically altered the form of his estimate this year. At page 49 the total amount to be voted is given in one lump sum, $4,107,000. Last year the estimates were spread over two and a half pages, carefully itemized by provinces, so that a member interested in one or more provinces could see at a glance what the expenditures were and with a certain degree of detail. My first question is:	What is the reason for this
change?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is no particular
reason for the change other than it makes the record more complete. I can assure the hon. member there was no ulterior motive in making the change from the former method. It has to deal with all matters pertaining to the Indians, and any member who has a question he wishes to bring up may discuss it as fully under the item as it stands at present as he could have done formerly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am quite sure there is no ulterior motive in the mind of the minister, but if the item is voted in this lump sum there is no definite destination directed by parliament. Therefore the department will have the power to swing the entire $3,000,000, or the bulk of it, within certain statutory limitations, to even one province. The different amounts not being designated by the house and voted in that way, certain sums may be diverted to the wrong provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member fears
that possibly under the vote as at present constituted, Indians living in one province might benefit at the expense of those living elsewhere. I can assure the hon. member that such a policy will not be followed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Can the
minister give me the total amount estimated as the expenditure required for Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories? They were includued in one column last year and the total then was $1,007,639.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The amount this year is

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there any decrease in the amount for the Blackfoot Indians?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the minister would give the amounts to be voted for each province, we would have a better idea of what the allocations are.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The estimates for each
province are as follows:
Nova Scotia,. $71,460; New Brunswick, $69,124; Prince Edward Island, $9,405; Ontario and Quebec, $359,411; Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories, $821,639; British Columbia, $489,600; Yukon, $21,450; General, $280,500; Indian education, including the construction of school buildings, $1,750,381. -Total, $3,873,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A reduction of $853,669.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is
estimated as being required for the Blackfoot agency in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Blackfoot agency, general expenses, $6,839.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That includes the requirements for the purpose of supplies for the agency, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It includes salaries, rations, travelling expenses of the agent, fuel and feed, miscellaneous and additions and repairs to buildings.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is the method of securing, let us say, the fuel supply? Is it by tender?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, by tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the
tender called for by advertisements?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not advertised; the
agent calls for tenders. [DOT]

Supply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The agent
does so privately; do I understand he does it himself?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On instructions from the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to have this clear. Is the invitation to tender
advertised?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, the tenders are not
advertised; they are not published advertisements.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Exactly;
may I ask the minister how it is done?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The procedure followed
for many years is being carried out; firms dealing in certain supplies are asked to tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suppose
a coal firm would be asked to supply coal. I just wish to have the matter clear, because this is an interesting point. I presume only coal firms would be asked to supply the coal for the agency.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be the natural inference, yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who was
awarded the contract this year for the Black-foot Indian agency?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not that information with me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the
answer given earlier in the session be correct, namely, that it was William McConnell of Gleichen?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not that information before me. Again, however, the inference is that it is correct, unless an error was made.-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to
direct the attention of the committee to a rather strange situation. The department does not advertise or call for tenders by advertisement. It appears that tenders are invited; by whom, I am not yet clear. Tenders were not invited from all the coal dealers in the town of Gleichen where the coal was purchased. Certain selected favourites are invited to tender, and in addition some who are not in the coal business at all and never have been are requested to tender. It may interest the committee and surprise the minister-because I am quite sure he is not a party to this-that this year's contract was awarded to a man who is not and never was a coal dealer, and that two of the regular firms dealing in coal in the town were not consulted or asked to tender. The man who got the contract is
purchasing the coal from the Crown Lumber Company. I understand-and I trust my information is correct-that cheques in payment for the coal are being made out to Mr. McConnell, who, I presume, in turn pays the Crown Lumber Company for the coal shipped in.
But that is not all. This year's tender for the coal is $7.65 f.o.b. agency; $7.65 at farm No. 2 at Cluny; $8.65 at farm No. 3; $9.25 at farm A and $9.65 at farm B,-a five mile haul. We may take it, therefore, that the base price laid down f.oib. the agency is $7.65. It happens there is another government department in the town, namely, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They also sent out invitations for tenders, and probably through some accident the wrong person got an opportunity to tender, a person who has been tendering for about fifteen years, and whose figure was the regular market rate. That tender was for first grade jewel coal-and there is no better-to be laid down at Gleichen at $6.40 a ton.
The mystery to me is why a man who is not a coal dealer should get a contract for three hundred tons of coal. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police order was for only twelve tons, and hon. members will readily see how valueless such an order would be. That contract, however, is filled at the rate of $6.40 per ton, which is a fair price when we consider the drop in coal prices in the present year and the further drop in the costs of handling. On the other hand the Indian agency, which does not invite tenders by advertising but selects certain privileged persons who are asked to tender, awards a contract at $7.65 per ton, or $125 more than was necessary. That is worth while considering. The gentleman in question, Mr. McConnell, is the president of the local Conservative association. That is indeed most interesting.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But not a crime.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not a crime. It is very interesting, however, that the president of a Conservative association, who is not a -coal dealer, should be awarded a contract at $125 above the price at which coal could be secured. But that is not all. This government has been spending money in the development of a coal mine on the Indian agency. In 1929 the sum of only $56.11 was spent; in 1930 $100.56 was spent; in 1931,- there was a real -boom on at that time-the government spent $2,193. That is the information I have received from the department. There is a similar difference in the output. In the year 1929 the output was only 260 tons; in 1930, 600 tons; in 1931, 3,085 tons. The Indian agent is selling the coal, in the town
Supply-Indian Affairs

of Gleichen where the agency is situated. That is first grade lump coal, and is being sold at $3 a ton. Now comes a further mystery: Why does the agent go outside the district to buy coal from the president of a Conservative association at $125 above the hauled-in price of domestic coal in Drumheller when he has at his own door a mine developed and operated and worked by Indians under the supervision of the department producing 3,085 tons, which is being sold around the district for only $3 a ton? I leave to the minister the elucidation of these mysteries. I am sure he is not a party to such irregularities, but I do hope he will clear up the mess. Certainly the situation is not a pleasant one in the nostrils of the people of that district. It is an affront both to good Conservatives and to people of other political persuasions, and is the sort of practice which should not be permitted to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not all the facts before me, but I do not think the matter is as mysterious as the hon. member may think. It may be that the man who secured the tender did so at a price slightly higher-about a dollar a ton, if I followed the hon. member correctly. The fact, however, that there was a haulage of some five miles or more, would no doubt explain the difference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the minister does not wish to mislead the committee. The coal which was hauled five miles cost $9.65 per ton, an amount greatly in excess of $6.40.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is haulage in each
case?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is no haulage for agency coal laid down at Gleichen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not hauled a certain distance?

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
About three-quarters of a mile, or about the same distance as it would ibe to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police barracks.
Mr, MURPHY: As the hon. member is well aware, there are many different grades of coal sold in western Canada. The haulage may explain part of the difference. I do not say it does; I am offering it as one explanation because I have not all these details before me. But with , regard to the other matter of which he complains, namely, that the Indians have on their reserve a coal mine, I do know that is true. I may tell the hon. member that the mine was opened up under the present administration. Whereas formerly the department bought their coal outside, now that the mine on that reserve has been opened up it

is not only supplying the fuel needs of the Indians themselves, but also, I believe those of the agency this fall. I may also say to the hon. .member that we received some very strong protests against the present policy of the department in operating that mine for the benefit of the Indians. The Indians have not only been able to supply themselves with fuel, but they have been given work during all last winter at fair wages. They have also been able to purchase coal at the mine head, merely paying the wage cost, and selling it, as he said, in the town at $3 a ton. This is directly of benefit to the Indians-something they did not have until the mine was opened Aout a year or so ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Since the mine is producing 3,085 tons of coal, and, as the minister states, he hopes to produce a greater quantity next year, why is his department purchasing coal from outside at more than twice the amount? Is that economic? Is it common sense? If the Canadian National Railway system was run on that basis it would be broke long ago.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I stated, the mine has been open only a few months, and it may be that the department was not in a position at the time-I speak again subject to correction -to supply its needs. In other words, the tenders were called for for the season 1931-32, prior to the opening of the mine. But now that we are in a position to meet those requirements, there is no reason why the coal should not be supplied to the agency from the mine provided it is suitable coal for their requirements.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister h moment ago attempted to show that there might be some explanation for this thing. I happen to know that the coal that was ten-tered for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was a very fine, first class grade of domestic coal. You could not get anything better. It is the bottom seam coal. It is laid down at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police barracks at $6.40 a ton and only for twelve tons.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was a gift.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They did not have the advantage of getting it in carload lots as they can for the agency order, which amounts to 300 tons. I am glad the minister is open to reason in this matter. I do hope ihe will look into it, because frankly it is a disgrace. I cannot imagine anything that more reeks of the old spoils system than this thing does. The government takes office, pro-

ceeds to develop a coal mine on the reserve, produces a tremendous quantity this year, knew it was going to do so because it spent 82,193 in 1931, in addition to $56.11 in 1929 and $100.50 in 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the hon. member will bear me out when I say that the mine at that time was not producing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not anything like the quantity that is being produced today.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not anything at all, I think.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was some coal being taken out in 1930. The facts are as I have stated to the minister. The government changes office, the new government does not call for tenders by advertisement, but sends out an invitation to one or two friends in the town, and accepts a tender from one of those men, whom obviously they must have had their eyes upon all the time, or whose eyes must have been upon them all the time-the president of the local Conservative association. He gets the contract at a price that is higher than any price contracted for in the district by a government agency since 1928. Remember that. During all the period the price of coal has been going down. In 1928 it was $7.50; in 1929, $7.20; in 1930, $7.20; in 1931, $6.40. I am sure hon. members are fully as disturbed as I am about this matter and do not like this kind of thing to be done with public money. This gentleman may be a very worthy man, but why the government should have given the contract to him for a large amount of coal, 300 tons, at $1.25 over the price at which they could have secured first grade coal, is a mystery to me. Of course, the other point is that the man is not a coal dealer, and never has been-. Again, for fear there may be any mistake about it, the price paid to this gentleman is $7.65 f.o.b. agency, which gives him a profit of $1.25 for doing nothing except signing a contract. On farm No. 2, Cluny- which is also in the same relation to the railway station as the Gleichen farm-the same price is quoted, $7.65; at farm No. 3, which is one mile away, the price-full allowance has been made for providing profit-is $8.65, at farm A, four miles away, the price is $9.25, and at farm B, five miles away, the price is $9.65. I can assure the minister that the contract is well worth while; it has not cost any effort or investment on the part of him who got it. It is a straight gift out of the public treasury and is a disgrace. I know the minister will pay attention to the matter and have it cleaned up.
Supply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there a man by the name of William Tweed well, Indian agent at Le Pas, where there is a reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was a William Tweedwell, at Le Pas.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was he dismissed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For what reason?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: For incompetency and misbehaviour.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was the misbehaviour political partisanship?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was a man by the name of Samuel Lovell appointed agent in the place of Tweedwell?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is acting temporarily.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the position been advertised?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not think so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will it be advertised by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It may not be advertised, for this reason; an order in council was passed some time last year directing the Civil Service Commission to fill vacancies by appointing former members of the Department of the Interior staff who in their opinion had the necessary qualifications to fill such offices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is my information correct, that the only qualification of this man Lovell is that he is a painter by trade?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no information on
that subject.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the minister let
me have that information as soon as possible? My information is that this man Tweedwell was dismissed for very poor reasons, and I believe the minister and his department were skating on very thin ice in making that dismissal. Then they temporarily appointed a man who I am told has had no experience in that line of work, whose trade is that of painter. The Indians might need a little warpaint or something like that, but I should like the minister to give me that information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think it is in the public interest or in the interest of any employee of the government to state publicly, in certain cases, everything that might be said against that individual, but I can assure my hon. friend that if he will come to the office of the department and consult the files he will not repeat the statement he made a
Supply-Indian Affairs

few moments ago, that we were skating on very thin ice in dismissing this man. I do not wish to pursue the subject at greater length for the reasons I have already given, but if the hon. member persists it may not be greatly to his advantage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I might tell the minister that since this government has been in power there have been so many dismissals for political partisanship, and the investigators have condemned men on such scanty evidence, that members on this side of the house must be expected to be suspicious. Among those dismissed from the Post Office Department or from the minister's own department I could name many who have been dismissed or suspended because of charges of political partisanship, many of which were cooked. In my own district we had an investigator inquiring into the conduct of a civil servant accused of political partisanship, whose accuser was a mail contractor, delivering the mail from the station to the post office, who acted as agent for the Conservative candidate. This was the man who made the charge against the postmaster, whom he was trying to get dismissed. If I can get the information I require privately I will do so.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no knowledge at
all of anything that might have taken place with regard to the Post Office Department, but I can assure the hon. member that no charge of political partisanship was made in the case of the agent who was retired at Lc Pas.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will give the minister some information that he may remember. A certain medical man who was attending the Indians on a reserve in my district was advised shortly after the election was over, that his services were no longer required. That man never took any part in the campaign; I warned him not to do so. I feared that the promises my hon. friends were making might bring them into power, so I told him, "If you do not take any part in this fight you will be able to hold your position." He did not take any part, but nevertheless in October or November he was notified that his services were no longer required. That dismissal was unjust and unfair, and it has turned more votes away from my hon. friends opposite than anything else they could do in my district.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In fairness to the
minister and to the gentleman referred to by the hon. member for Provencher, I think I should say a word, since probably I am
[Mr Murphy.]
in a better position to know about this matter than any man in this house. Mr. Twecdwell was a very warm supporter of mine, so there could be hardly any partisanship shown in his dismissal. Mr. Tweedwell was looking upon the wine when it was red just a little too much; he got himself into difficulties, an investigation was requested and an investigator was sent up. I have not seen the evidence on which he was dismissed, but I can assure the hon. member for Provencher that the department had every justification for the action that was taken.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
AVhen these estimates
were under consideration last year I asked the minister a question regarding the list of firms permitted to tender on supplies for the Indians. I mentioned the specific case of a firm in connection with the supplying of flour to the Indians in northern Saskatchewan. For many years the Bishop Milling Company of the town of Battleford supplied flour to the Indians, not only under the late government but under the preceding government as well. Last year I asked why the Bishop Milling Company was not permitted now to tender for flour; in fact I wrote the minister's department, and I was told then that they were not on what I might call the eligible list. Might I ask the minister whether they are on that list now, and if they are not on it would the minister tell me why they are not.
Mr. MUItPHY: I am not sure whether the firm mentioned by the hon. member has been asked to tender, but I am safe in saying that there is a firm in Battleford that is asked to submit prices. I am not certain whether or not it is the firm he mentioned a moment ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the deputy minister the information?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am informed that the Bishop Milling Company is asked to tender on supplies.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to thank the
minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like the minister to be good enough to revert for a moment to a question of policy. In my riding I have two Indian bands, and on the average I think they are as intelligent as the ordinary citizen of the country. Most of them are equally thrifty and ambitious, and many of them have expressed the wish to me, both individually and collectively, that they might become enfranchised and enjoy the full rights of ordinary citizens. They harm never been able to do so, and for the life of me I cannot see why that should be so. A number of them went to the

Supply-Indian Affairs
war and were enfranchised as a result, but their brothers, their fathers, their mothers and their sisters are still there. They are ambitious, energetic and thrifty, and are very desirous of getting the citizenship that is enjoyed by other people in this country. I should like to ask the minister if it would not be possible to give these people a little more responsibility and a little more liberty by granting them full citizenship. I do not see why a difference in colour should bar one man from full citizenship while his neighbour enjojrs that privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I think the hon. member is aware, there is a provision in the Indian Act now whereby an Indian man or woman may be enfranchised, and Indians in different parts of Canada are being enfranchised practically all the time. It is done by order in council, after certain recommendations have been made in regard to the standing, the character and the ability of the person concerned. To the best of my knowledge there is no provision in the Indian Act now whereby Indians might be enfranchised en bloc. That could only be done if the present Indian Act were amended. The question has been given some consideration but not all the consideration it deserves, and it may well be that legislation might be introduced in this house to accomplish something of what the hon. member has in mind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank the minister
for his assurance that consideration will be given. I was quite well aware of the provisions he has enumerated, but in the fifteen years I have been in this house I have been able to get only one enfranchised, and that took me from six months to a year. Speaking irrespective of governments, I do not think this matter has received in the past the consideration which the citizens in those bands deserve. I thank the minister for the promise that the matter will be considered, because I think it is just that it should be.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was very much
pleased to hear the minister say that the department had been successful in arranging with the government of Quebec for granting exclusive rights to Indians in that province to take furbearing animals north of the Transcontinental railway, and if I understood him correctly he said that at present an effort was being made, pending the report of the game commission appointed in Ontario some eighteen months ago, to accomplish the same object in the province of Ontario, namely, to provide that north of the Transcontinental railway the Indians should have the exclusive right in that
province. So far as the Indians north of the Transcontinental are concerned, that would be a splendid arrangement. But what about the Indians south of the Transcontinental? There are two distinct bands or, as they are sometimes referred to, tribes of Indians in the northern part of Ontario and the eastern part of Manitoba. To some extent, particularly in northern Ontario, the Cree Indians found their native home north of the height of land in the watersheds of the Hudson bay, while the Ojibway Indians found their home south of the height of land, roughly speaking. If the Cree Indians get their rights north of the Transcontinental they will be amply taken care of, but they would be about in the same position north of the height of land if an attempt were made to transport the Ojibway bands of Indians from the watershed of the great lakes to north of the Transcontinental, which is only a small portion of Hudson bay watershed, because the watershed comes down one hundred miles south of the Transcontinental. The hunting grounds south of the Transcontinental are more prolific and will furnish better opportunities for the Indians, in the main, than the hunting grounds north of the Transcontinental. You will take care of one group of Indians partially, namely, the Crees, north of the Transcontinental, but the Crees south of the Transcontinental in the watershed of the great lakes will be in the position they are now in-and their position is worse than that of any Indians I know of in the country. There are three lines of railways traversing the districts from end to end of that country, and it is through these railway lines that the white hunter comes in. Then, following up what the hon. member for St. Boniface has said with regard to the Indians not being permitted to take furbearing animals or food supplies from the game in Manitoba, certainly they are not in Ontario; they are treated exactly the same as the while man is treated. They are haled before the police court if they shoot a partridge out of season, or for any act committed in violation of the game laws of Ontario, just the same as any white man. The result is that they have been reduced to a state of absolute pauperism, their only means of earning a living having been taken away from them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I suggest that a slight mistake has been made in curtailing the description of the votes. If it was desirable to have the vote all in one item, then at least the items the minister read to the committee allocating certain amounts to each province should be in the
Supply-Indian Affairs

estimates. However, that is not the point I want to make at present. Will the minister give some explanation with regard to the closing of the Regina office and the allocation of the three inspectors?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The commissioner's office
at Regina, as such, has been closed and Inspector Murison will continue, under the department here at Ottawa, in charge of affairs in Saskatchewan, Inspector Hamilton in Winnipeg for the province of Manitoba, and Inspector Christianson in Calgary for the province of Alberta.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Reporting
direct to Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Reporting direct to Ottawa, yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the curtailment of the amount allocated generally to the department, how much of the reduction is estimated to be in construction of schools? Perhaps I might put it a better way:	Are there any new schools under construction this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Any new
hospitals?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I understand that what is known as the Greater Production Farm in the neighbourhood of Regina has been abandoned. What was the reason for this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As nearly as I have been able to ascertain, what is known as the Greater Production Farm was brought into existence, along with some others of a similar type, during the war years when this country was straining every effort to provide foodstuffs for the allied armies. In other years a similar farm was closed on the Blood reserve in Alberta. This year it was decided to close the farm north of Regina, because the Indian department is not engaged in the business of farming as such; that is rather outside the province of the department. I may say, for the information of the hon. member, that the farm has not been abandoned. An arrangement has been entered into with the former manager of the farm whereby he will crop the land this year with the idea eventually, in a couple of years' time, of returning the farm to its natural grassy state to obviate the danger of the land becoming weedy and thus a menace to surrounding farms.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Has any of this land
been handed over to the Indians to farm this year, or has it been placed in the hands of this individual to carry on farming?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The arrangement has been made with the individual to farm the area with the idea of returning the land to its natural grassy state, or to sow the land where needed to broom or some other variety of grass.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Can the minister advise
the committee of the present stage of the negotiations between himself or his department and the government of Quebec with regard to Indian reservation lands alienated by this government? The privy council has decided that these lands must revert to the provinces and that the proceeds of any sales belong to the provinces. I understand there is now due to the province of Quebec more than S300,000 in proceeds from the sales of these lands. I think an arrangement was reached many years ago with the province of Ontario, but so far no definite conclusion has been reached as far as Quebec and the Dominion government are concerned. I understand that the department take the stand that the province must wait; they do not contest the validity of the claim but they seem to ask for some sort of moratorium. The province of Quebec in the past has been willing to agree to favours being granted to other provinces; it does not ask for any favours, but it has a right to the money received from the sale of Indian lands which are the property of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in one
sense, I am rather pleased that the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has brought up this question. I have not all the details before me, but I think the general facts are something like these: It was understood by the Dominion government and by the Indians themselves that where a band surrendered a portion of their reserve for sale or lease, the proceeds of the sale would be held by the Dominion government in trust for the purpose of assisting the Indians. Certain lands in the province of Quebec were sold after being legally surrendered by the Indians to the department for disposal, and the province has claimed the reversionary interest in those lands. A case was carried to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, which decided that the province was entitled to the reversionary interest in the lands or, in other words, that the proceeds from the

Supply-Indian Affairs
sale of the lands belonged to the province. I do not dispute that that is the correct legal position, but certain negotiations have been carried on between the Premier of Quebec and myself and other officials of the government. The dominion's standpoint is that the province of Quebec could claim a reversionary interest in the lands. However, it may be of interest to the committee to know that the province of Ontario has entered into an agreement with the Dominion government whereby the proceeds of any such sales would be held in trust by the Dominion government to be used for the welfare of the Indians, and 1 have endeavoured to have the province of Quebec adopt a similar attitude. The Dominion government is not holding these moneys for the benefit of the crown in the right of the dominion; it is holding them in trust to be expended from time to time for the benefit of the Indians. I think there is a difference of opinion as to the $300,000 mentioned by the former Minister of Justice, the Dominion contending that that amount includes not only the proceeds from the sale of lands but also the proceeds from the sale of timber and other resources upon the lands. My main object has been to have the province of Quebec adopt the same attitude as that adopted by the province of Ontario, whereby the moneys from the sale of , such lands would remain with the Dominion government to be expended for the benefit of the Indian. If this is not done, the department will be placed in this position: Unless an Indian band dies out or for some reason leaves its reserve, no further land would be surrendered by the Indians, because it would be felt that the proceeds of any sales would go to the province and the poor Indian would be denied that which he supposed was his for all time to come.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not challenge the right of the minister to enter into negotiations with the province of Quebec to try to get them to agree, that this money should be kept in trust for the benefit of the Indians, but my hon. friend must agree that the money now in the hands of the government is the property of the province of Quebec. While negotiations are pending and before an agreement is reached, if it is ever reached, I do not think it is a fair method of procedure for the government to keep this money, and I do not see how my hon, friend can justify it. In order to show the view taken in regard to this matter by the government of the province of Quebec, I shall read the last fetter sent to my
hon. friend by the Premier and Attorney General of the province. The letter is dated April 25, and reads:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 19th instant, regarding the question of the property rights of the province of Quebec in lands comprising Indian reserves.
I regret to state that it is impossible for our government to accept the views expressed by you in your letter.
Surely, undisputed claims between Canadian governments cannot be treated in this way. After much litigation the privy council held, in the Star-Chrome case, that these lands reverted to the provinces.
Before this decision was rendered, the government of the dominion had been selling these lands. We declared, however, before the privy council that we w-ere prepared to recognize the validity of the titles given by Ottawa before the priviy council decision, and ever since Ottawa has been disposing of the lands, the proceeds of the sale being deposited in a special trust fund. The amount due the province of Quebec is now over three hundred thousand dollars, in addition to interest. We have, however, declared that we were prepared to waive interest if .the capital is paid forthwith.
I really cannot understand the stand that you take when you declare, in your letter, that the adjustment of this claim must be indefinitely deferred.
The government of the dominion is showing itself most generous for the provinces of the west and, for this generosity. I am offering no criticism. We are not applying for charity or for a gift, but only for the payment of a sum which is legitimately due to the province.
I. therefore, earnestly hope that our claim will be adjusted forthwith.
May I add that the privy council dealt with this matter in the ease of the Dominion of Canada vs. the province of Ontario, in 1910, in the Indian Treaties indemnity case. You will find that case reported at page 676 of Cameron's Canadian Constitution.
Yours truly,
L. A. Taschereau.
Ido not want to press the matter unduly, but I submit, even after the explanations of the minister, it is clear that the money belongs to the province of Quebec, and until any other agreement is reached and pending any negotiations, I dispute the right of this government to keep the money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I stated a few moments ago, there is no question, or at least I have never heard any, as to the legal right of the province of Quebec to the proceeds from the sale of the land. When the ex-minister read from the letter that settlement must be indefinitely postponed, this had reference to the amount claimed, not to the legal right of the province to the proceeds from the sale of the land. That is, the province of Quebec claims the right to money which was received from the sale of timber and certain other proceeds
Supply-Indian Affairs

which the Dominion government feels is not included in the judgment given by the privy council. But the ex-minister, in his concluding remarks, stated that he felt that this government was not entitled to keep moneys which rightfully belong to the province of Quebec, although we were endeavouring to negotiate with them whereby the moneys from the sale of this land would be kept for the Indians. That money has been owing to the province of Quebec for some years, I believe, and the ex-Minister of Justice, although I am not sure of this, may have had the matter brought to his attention during those years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not hear of it until two days ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Bad staff work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then I do not need to give any further explanation along that line. I sincerely hope, however, the province of Quebec will see its way clear to allow the dominion to retain that money in order that, it may be expended for the welfare of the Indians who certainly need it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think I should lend some support to the minister in this matter, because I had a rather trying experience with the province of Ontario in regard to the same question. While there is no use in denying the fact that we were defeated in the case .before the privy council, the question of ownership of Indian lands is rather beclouded. I always held the opinion that our case was not very well presented. It, however, went against us; there is no use in arguing about that, but even so, we felt we had a claim in equity. Surely these lands were set aside in the various provinces for the maintenance of Indians and the responsibility for their maintenance devolves upon the federal authorities. All the contributions the provinces made were the lands themselves.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The lands themselves- that is something.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-the lands themselves, for the purpose of setting aside reserves for the Indians. The care, the education and all the other responsibilities fell upon the shoulders of the federal government. It is not fair to say that there is any difference between the treatment in Ontario and Quebec and that in the western provinces, because under the agreement with the prairie provinces and British Columbia there is a provision that if further lands are required, they are prepared, upon negotiation, to provide them. If in the provinces sales of land are undertaken, the proceeds remain in the custody

of the federal government. It sems to me -this is a question of equity, if not of law. In the negotiations with the Ontario government we were able to retain these moneys and arrangements are made whereby, in sales of reserves in that province, the proceeds remain in the custody of the Department of Indian Affairs for the benefit of the Indians themselves. It is true on a clear case of law the province of Quebec is entitled to recover that money, but to be fair to the rest of the provinces and to give the same treatment-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quebec is paying all the time to the other provinces.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want to enter into a controversy with my hon. friend over that question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We shall discuss it at some other time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not particularly with respect to Indians-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We do not borrow money, but we want what is due to us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As regards the question of Indian reserves in Quebec, it is only fair to expect that that province should be given the same treatment as that which prevails in regard to Ontario.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the difficulty is
this: the ex-Minister of Justice overlooks the fact that the privy council has not decided that the fund, if it is paid to the province of Quebec, does not become a trust fund for the benefit of the Indians.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let Quebec decide that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If it is a trust fund for the benefit of the Indians, then as the exMinister of the Interior has observed, a difficulty of administration arises, because, under the constitution, with the dominion rests the responsibility for the Indians, and the extent to which the moneys thus received by the province from the sale of assets belonging to the Indians would pro tanto be available for their relief and support. I think what the exMinister of the Interior has said should be viewed from that standpoint. I understand the minister has suggested to Quebec, not that the moneys should not be paid in accordance with the terms of the judgment, but that, if paid, they should be regarded as a trust which may be administered by the dominion or by the province, but if by the province, by its discharging the constitutional obligation of the dominion with respect to the wards of the crown, namely, the Indians.

Sup-ply-Indian Affairs

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does my right hon. friend not think that, while these negotiations are pending, the money should go to the province to which it belongs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The question has not been determined, as I understand it-

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
not heard my sentence. The question has not been determined whether or not the money is earmarked as a trust fund, and if paid over by the dominion without its being thus earmarked, a question that might be very difficult would arise. That is the point which the minister has endeavoured to make with the provincial authorities. If we earmark it as a trust fund, then of course the administration of the fund would relieve pro tanto the obligations of the dominion. But this would complicate administration, because you would have the province charged with a responsibility which constitutionally rests with	us.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Surely the	judgment	is
clear that when Indian lands are abandoned, they , revert to the provinces.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When they	are	sold,	the
money should go to the province, whether that money is earmarked or not. Whether it is to be administered for the benefit of the Indians or not, it must go to the province, and while this question is being discussed, I do not think it is fair on the part of the federal government to keep the money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Has the minister any
information with regard to the situation in relation to trachoma on the different reserves in the west?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not hear the hon.
member very well, but I believe he is inquiring about the trachoma situation in the west. At the present time the department is availing itself of the services of Doctor Wall, who is an expert in that disease, having especially studied the subject in Vienna. He is making a tour throughout the west and is instructing the various doctors whose services were engaged for the benefit of the Indians in the detection and treatment of this disease. He is cooperating also with the provincial Departments of Health in their endeavour to prevent the ravages of that disease among certain elements of the white population.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was very much interested in the questions asked by the hon. member for Bow River concerning the coal 41761-163
contract at Gleichen. I have before me a return which was tabled in this house some time ago at the request of the hon. member. Notwithstanding the fact that the price of coal has been very substantially reduced, I notice the department is paying fifteen cents per ton more than they did in the previous year. Can the minister explain this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have already informed the committee that tenders were asked for by the Indian agent, and that the lowest tender was accepted. Further than that I can give no explanation to the committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the minister really believe that they were proper tenders? In his own mind is he satisfied that those tenders were properly made?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They were proper, I
suppose, in the sense that they were submitted by responsible dealers. When those dealers were tendering they knew that they were in a competitive field, and as business men they would know that they must submit prices at which they could supply the coal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In view of the fact that the public was not asked to tender for the supply of coal I presume the minister would not like to say that the tenders were really competitive?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister would not for one moment say that those tenders were competitive; the public was not asked to tender for the supplying of coal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, the tenders were competitive, because the different dealers were asked to quote. I do not know what the hon. member has in mind when he suggests to the committee that those men got together in some sort of cabal and boosted the price. I do not know whether or not that is what the hon. member has in mind. Apart from that, however, I would say that as business men they would submit the lowest possible prices in order to secure the business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not infer that those gentlemen got together with the idea of boosting the price higher than it should have been. In an endeavour to get to the bottom of this matter I should like to ask the minister how many tendered for the coal contract, the amounts at which they tendered, and the dates upon which the tenders were received.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am sorry I.have not that information before me.

Supply-Indian Affairs

Mr, GARDINER: I do not like to delay the item, yet I should not like to see it pass until we have some further explanation in regard to so important a matter. After all, we are spending the funds of the people, and it is the duty of this house to see to it that proper tenders are received. In all cases, quality considered, the lowest tenderer should receive the contract. In this particular instance it is quite evident that only a few people were asked to tender. I believe the committee would be justified in asking the minister to let the item stand until such time as he can furnish more information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to know who were invited to tender for this coal contract. I should like to have the tenders produced, so that the committee may know whether the lowest tender was accepted, the date that tenders were asked for and when the successful tender was accepted, in order that we may determine whether or not the agency itself could have supplied this coal from its own mine at the time the tenders *were received.
I should like to say a word or two about the manner in which estimates have been brought before the committee this year, as compared with that of former years. In item 201 of this year's estimates a lump sum of 83,873,000 is provided. If hon. members will turn to last year's estimates they will find a much better description of the particular purposes for which these moneys are allocated than is to be found in the estimates now before us. With all the estimates for the Department of Indian Affairs lumped in one sum it is quite possible for the department to allocate those funds to whatever purpose they may desire. Under the circumstances and in view of my past experience I do not think that is advisable. Turning to page 54 of the estimates for the year 1931-32, last year, we find that there are certain amounts allocated to each of the provinces, and the total vote was $4,516,313. Then we come to a special vote for Nova Scotia, and in that vote there is a sum set aside for salaries, another for supplies for destitute Indians, another to provide for encouragement of agriculture, another for medical attendance and medicines, another for repairs to roads and dyking, another for Indian dwellings, and the last for miscellaneous and unforeseen expenditures. Each of these items has a certain amount of money allocated to it in last year's estimates, making a total for the province of Nova Scotia of 885,960.

maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that it is now eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-CANNED SALMON INSPECTION STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the committee rises I should like to make one or two observations. When the hon. member for Bow River first raised the question of coal I said I had not the particulars before me. When I replied to the hon. member for Acadia I was speaking generally, as to the policy of the department in connection with tenders, and I made the assertion that the lowest tender is accepted. At that time I was not speaking of the particular case to which the hon. member had directed his remarks, but was referring to the general practice in the department. May I add that at the next sitting I shall have the necessary information for hon. members opposite.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, May 3, 1932.
